reviews.author: Filipe Furtado
reviews.text: Famke Janssen is under house arrest for killing her abusive cop husband, so of course the place is hunted by him so filmmaker Eric Red can make the stalked by the ex from hell scenario as literal as possible. Red has always been more of a writer than director and his movies tend to operate under similar genre high concepts, but a lot of the choices here are worse than usual and a lot of it is Janssen alone in the house while paranormal stuff happens, and it isn’t engrossing enough to work. There are a few possible good ideas on the periphery, but despite some solid work from Janssen and Bobby Cannavale, very few of them take hold.

reviews.text: You know what director Marcus Koch is good at filming? Violence. The scenes in this movie of an obese clown, Gurdy, carrying out a killing spree, armed mainly with a big fuck-off meat cleaver, and chopping numerous people's limbs, heads, faces, hands and feet off, are thrilling and enthralling, if you're a fan of splattery excess like I am. It doesn't even matter that the victims are almost entirely characters who've been introduced mere moments before their demises. The special effects, created by a team headed by Koch himself, and a banging techno score by Kristian Day & Carl Homer, add to the brilliant brutality.

reviews.author: Reilly
reviews.text: Gamers rise up. A loving homage to the youtuber star vehicle feature films of the early 2010s, akin to John Carpenter's many tributes to Howard Hawks. Sports movie cliches and out of focus shots are used to great effect to further the film's points on digital media, modern consumerism, and intersectionality, with thought provoking results. The power of video games might be bringing together an improbably diverse group of young women defined by broad comedic archetypes, but the power of cinema is to make us think. Think about things like the wonderful delivery options at Pizza Hut, or the all new Mercedes-Benz GLV 350. A strong contender for the boldest new release of 2022.

reviews.author: Lyncoln
reviews.text: Near the end of World War II, set in Japan, Tokiko Tanaka is a woman waiting for her husband's return while taking care of her son in a country facing an economic crisis, where financial hardship haunts households. When her son has a serious constipation and ends up in the hospital for 10 days, Tokiko is unable to pay the bill, having already sold many belongings from her home. In desperation, she chooses to prostitute herself to get the money. After her husband returns, she confesses what happened, sending him into a state of shock.

reviews.author: Cindy_J
reviews.text: One of the more undervalued Ozu films, A Hen in the Wind offers a bleak but compassionate picture of postwar Japanese masculinity and of the ordeals faced by those at home during and after the war. The scene in which Tanaka's husband confronts her about what she had to do in his absence in order to save their child's life is harrowing in its intensity. More than any other film he made, A Hen in the Wind proves that Ozu could also do melodrama! Kinuyo Tanaka is terrific as always.

reviews.author: Darren Carver-Balsiger
reviews.text: A Hen in the Wind is a very distinct Ozu film, featuring some of his most brutal scenes. Set in the ruins of Japan at the end of World War Two, the film is initially about poverty and desperation. The film then moves into intense melodrama, featuring prostitution and marital violence. A Hen in the Wind is a harsh tale about a conservative and repressed Japanese society. It isn't directly political, but presents an understanding of the different perspectives people can have on painful topics, while showing a lot of sympathy to suffering women. A candid conversation with a prostitute makes clear the unfortunate situation many women found themselves in. A Hen in the Wind centres on a married couple…

reviews.text: Wow what a film that felt like a gut punch. I really felt reticent to watch this and it took me till the twenty minute mark to flip my switch of being engaged with the material. The premise is simple but the delivery is so cleverly cleaved in two (and sometimes three with the kid) with just a smart visual aspect. Honestly the husband rushing halfway down the stairways to ask his wife if she is okay knowing all the pain she has gone through and endures just breaks me and might just be my strongest movie moment of the year. It deals with his issues of modernity(as always) but really focuses on family and relationships with friends with an understanding that only can be built through time and development.It does have a bookend shot and I do love those because I feel we see life progressed through the viewers eyes. Don't sleep on this one it's a Ozu gem

reviews.author: Enfant du Siècle
reviews.text: Kaze no naka no mendori is a quite particular film within Yasujirō Ozu's filmography; although formally made with the Japanese director's distinctive formal rigor, the plot and some of its themes are closer to something one would expect to find in a work by Kenji Mizoguchi. On this occasion, Ozu focuses his attention on the precariousness and sacrifices of the women who tried to subsist during the war, their longing for happy days, the attempt to cope with the absence of a husband who was at the front, and the marital problems they have to confront upon his return. reviews.text: The good Christopher Guest movies are the ones that reflect a deep and textured knowledge of the milieu they depict. Guest obviously doesn't know shit about the world of professional mascot performers (does such a "community" even exist???), but he clearly knows a lot about folk music, and has opinions about it. Something I like about this movie is that the three folk acts — the Folksmen, Mitch & Mickey, and the (New) Main Street Singers — aren't even really "authentic." They're all shitty, sanitized, commercial bastardizations of whatever folk music originally was before the big labels came after it. I especially like that, even though the Folksmen are shitty hacks, they still regard the New Main Street Singers with disdain…

reviews.author: Sydney🚀
reviews.text: Not surprised at all by how intensely people are bouncing off this, the subject matter obviously invites specific readings of/distastes for the film when it surely would be easier to swallow as a melodrama without that. I still really enjoyed it because it makes the relieving decision to not center around whether the assault really happened, but how the people involved react and why. It’s intentionally incredibly knotty, no character is painted as one thing, and the way all of their insecurities and lies they tell themselves come out in the terrible ways they communicate with each other is uncomfortable and confrontational. It’s still wincingly limited, but I think Nora Garrett’s screenplay is more aware of those limitations than people are giving it credit for. Many great closeups of faces and hands. Completely ridiculous in a way i found very yummy.

reviews.text: I love Hollywood gossip, always have, always will. If it involves the exploits of Errol Flynn and his swashbuckling cock, then I'm usually sold, despite Flynn's somewhat dodgy reputation for trying to shag almost every woman he met. He was linked to scandals, had numerous brushes with the law, and one court case against him for rape which nearly destroyed his career, and as his star waned, alcohol made him the shadow of his former self. This film for Universal, released in the December of 1952, saw Flynn donning the pirate gear once more, this time for director George Sherman, in what I believe was technically his fourth outing as a pirate? It's a colourful affair, rich and vibrant, with…

reviews.author: Quiller
reviews.text: This was the last swashbuckler Errol Flynn made in Hollywood — though he starred in a few more in Europe after relocating there. It pales in comparison to his masterpieces, like The Adventures Of Robin Hood, and he looks more tired and less athletic than he did just four years earlier in Adventures Of Don Juan (1948). He may have already been suffering from the hepatitis he was diagnosed with later in 1952. He still oozes his playful charm, though, and he gets solid support from Maureen O’Hara as his main love interest and Anthony Quinn as his main antagonist. If you’re a fan of Flynn’s work, it’s worth checking out once.

reviews.text: As far as swashbuckling films go this has to now be one of my absolute favourites. Errol Flynn is superb in the lead and even being later in his life he has all the charm and charisma as his early films. However for me it was Maureen O’Hara who truly stole the entire film she just commanded the screen and your attention. I adored that even in a male dominated world she knew what she wanted and never let any man tell her what to do nor take anything from her she wasn’t ready to give. The scene in which she finally tells Flynn she’s ready to be kissed with incredible confidence was so empowering to see. I honestly was surprised to see such a fantastic female character in a film from the 1950s I just wish I had a fraction of her confidence.

reviews.text: Stupidly well directed and tense for what is ultimately a pretty standard legacy sequel. Multiple sequences had me gripped and temporarily paralyzed with fear (shout out to the anti-gravity acid scene for being particularly unique) before I remembered "Oh yeah, I don't need to speculate about anyone's survival since I've seen the original Alien." It feels like a crime to waste Fede Álvarez, Cailee Spaeny, and David Jonsson's immense talents on something so predictable and unambitious, but I'd be lying if I said it wasn't really effective in a vacuum. I can imagine this being a good entry point to the series for newcomers, but if you have the choice, please seek out the original first.

reviews.text: An incredibly trite affair that feels at least a decade behind the times. No assured point of view. Struggles to be both an achingly earnest drama about a black family beset by death and dementia and homophobia and a satire that indicts the publishing industry and Hollywood about how blackness has become currency. But it lacks the finesse and the depth for either approaches to come anywhere close to their targets. Muddled as fuck. Directed and shot like the blandest ‘90s TV drama imaginable. An early aughts comedy show sketch stretched out to movie length. I was unsure of this going into it but this was much worse than I ever thought it was going to be. Unfunny, unfeeling, unthinking.

reviews.text: José Ramón Larraz is a bit of a hit or miss director who made some great films with 'Vampyres' and 'Symptoms' but also some fairly mediocre stuff. This Laura Gemser vehicle falls in the later category, but it's also not as terrible as I expected. It's sort of a sex comedy, but not in the super silly slapstick way most Italian sex comedies work. It's not that funny and goes for more of a 'coming of age' story about a teenage boy's encounters with his lesbian nurse neighbours, Laura Gemser and Barbara Rey. The story doesn't really go anywhere, but I guess that's part of the genre. The main reason to watch this is Laura Gemser and she does have a few good moments in this; especially the scenes with her and Barbara Rey are pretty sexy, and in the end that's what you come for.

reviews.author: Sean Gilman
reviews.text: The only relation I can see between this and the first Angel Terminators film is that they both exist in a universe that follows all our normal laws of physics except for the fact that objects have a tendency to catch fire and explode whenever they impact other objects despite an apparent lack of incendiary material. Instead of being a sequel or having any of the same stars or creative team (they share a producer, George Lai, who also produced Godfrey Ho’s Princess Madam) it reunites the stars of director Tony Lou Chun-ku’s 1991 film Dreaming the Reality (Moon Lee, Oshima Yukari, and Sibelle Hu) and throws them into a wild collection of action scenes that plays out something like the Girls with Guns A Better Tomorrow with a School on Fire twist.

reviews.author: More_Badass
reviews.text: Rewatching this, I saw a movie that I’d place among the best of mid ‘90s Hong Kong action. Angel Terminator 2 strikes such an intriguing pacing and tonal balance, with a first half marinating in crime-drama hang-out vibes to that point that some could call it boring yet also erupting into blistering violence every ten minutes or so. Nicely shot, consistently entertaining whether via action or character interactions, and packed with ferocious fights as light melodrama cauterizes into gritty bloodshed. A Dreaming The Reality reunion that gives its three leading ladies more engaging drama than most of its contemporaries, but also delivers the goods of a fiery badass Yukari Ôshima, Moon Lee kicking so much ass, and Sibelle Hu with a shotgun.

reviews.author: Paul Elliott
reviews.text: Latvian animation artist Gints Zilbalodis was only seventeen years old when he created this seven-minute short. It sees him taking advantage of the knowledge of cats being reluctant, often frighten by water - principally because felines pride themselves in their agility, and their movements in water become somewhat listless, which they find is an unnatural state. The story follows a cat awakening and finding themselves in an ocean and needing to learn to adjust very quickly to survive. The animation is the most primitive amongst his increasing filmography, but his experimentation with lighting ensures this was a stepping stone in the development of his style.

reviews.text: Als hätte Terrence Malick ein paar Monate mit Dreams verbracht und sich seinen eigenen "Journey meets Team Ico und Ghibli"-Film mitsamt Hans Zimmer-Gedächtnisscore gebastelt. Ja, die Animationen sind jetzt nicht so ganz geschmeidig, an die Grafik muss man sich gewöhnen und über die metaphorischen Qualitäten einzelner Szenen und Bilder kann man so viel streiten wie grübeln oder unbeeindruckt hinweg lächeln. Aber die Ruhe, die immer wieder toll anschwellende Musik, die atmosphärische Welt, die dynamische Kamera, die zum Teil erhabenen Sequenzen, die minimale, dennoch völlig ausreichende Mimik einzelner Figuren und die eben völlig wortlose Reise haben mich doch in ihren Bann gezogen. Oder innerlich so abheben lassen wie den Jungen beim letzen Crescendo. Kein Film der aktuellen Themen, mehr der essentiellen. Auf seine Art einfach, aber auch einfach schön.

reviews.text: For me, every Tennessee Williams adaptation I’ve seen on film carries a certain charge. His plays are so alive with detail, intelligent in their construction, and daring in how they explore desire, repression, and the darker corners of human behavior. Williams has always had a gift for writing characters that feel both painfully personal and thematically bold. With Baby Doll, Elia Kazan adapts two of Williams’ one-act plays "27 Wagons Full of Cotton" and "The Unsatisfactory Supper" and while it’s far from Kazan’s best work, it’s a film that earns its place by being unapologetically strange, uncomfortable, and undeniably Williams.

reviews.text: My boys James Woods and Yaphet Kotto are the DA team-up I never knew I needed in my life. Badge of the Assassin is a true-to-heart courtroom flick steeped in the cyclical patterns of the American justice system. This probably will seem dated to most folks today, but I actually find it incredibly relevant. There's a handshake that could have been more iconic than the Carl Weathers and Schwarzeneggar meme that gets tossed around these days--a celebratory moment that made me fist pump the air. reviews.text: By all accounts an 'anti-theo' film in so many ways (films that feel sufficiently "90s" like this and I do not tend to agree) and yet I can't help but fall for its ludicrous, juvenile charms. Mainly due to Barry Sonnenfeld's excellent direction and restless camera, the visual component of these sketch-comedy films which normally are lacking if (barely) serviceable finally catching up here to its manic script. Mercifully short too despite feeling like a whole-ass Odyssey, packing in an absurd amount of dialogue and setpieces involving an ensemble cast of over 15 in just under 80 minutes while never letting the viewer go for a single one. Probably not as good as I think it is, but films like this directed like this and with as much emphasis on sheer fun and chaos as this are genuinely few and far between. Perhaps the 90s aren't so bad after all.

reviews.author: Wesley Stenzel
reviews.text: Barry Sonnenfeld’s movies are almost always shot well and amazingly cast. Big Trouble is no exception to the trend — it’s a straightforwardly good-looking movie with an absolutely insane ensemble of character actors and rising stars, including Tim Allen, Stanley Tucci, Zooey Deschanel, Ben Foster, and Sofia Vergara. The movie never really finds its footing, as Sonnenfeld attempts to recapture the loose magic of Get Shorty with a much weaker script and a substantially shorter runtime. There are two bad dumb jokes for every good dumb joke, and the whole thing feels like a half-baked satire of post-9/11 culture in the US wrapped in a watered-down Tarantino/Elmore Leonard project. But the cast and style make it completely watchable, and it’s brisk enough to avoid becoming bothersome.

reviews.text: Provocar no es sinónimo de proponer. Al inicio de Blue boy, un entrevistado recita su autorización para aparecer en el documental, mientras que en los créditos finales oímos a otro exigir el pago que la producción prometió a cambio de su testimonio, y evidenciando que le están pidiendo algo (probablemente, aparecer en cámara) que no era parte del trato original. Cabría esperar que el cortometraje ahondase en cómo el cine reproduce la explotación de sus retratados para obras de supuesta denuncia, pero no sucede. Estos sonidos parecen estar ahí simplemente para incomodar, o para curarse en salud admitiendo su proceso de realización antes de que alguien acuse su ética cuestionable.

reviews.text: Provocante, poetico, teatral e intimista. Transitando por todos os membros desse intercâmbio, essa narrativa cria um mistério, uma neblina que até mesmo nas histórias contadas pelos setes jovens romenos se mantem oculta. As imagens estáticas, as cores e os enquadramentos criam uma atimosfera inerente, com um que que se desvela sem desvelar. Its two sister ships were Olympic and (most famously) Titanic. The sinking was nowhere near as devastating as Titanic’s as it resulted in 30 deaths as opposed to the 1500 on Titanic. It was still a tragedy no doubt, but definitely not all that notable (especially in the midst of World War 1)

Unlike the works of other actresses Rebecca Hall and Maggie Gyllenhaal who both did their first films this year, Berry undersells her directorial gift for a more conventional, accessible approach. Bruised concerns the story of a beaten down single mother who returns to MMA fighting in order to survive. There are short moments of great swagger and intensity behind the camera, but the handling of it needed a sturdier support and a cinematic flair to make it memorable—which this has none.

reviews.text: I started the film thinking it was just another one of my beloved prison escape sub-genres, but it was only after a few minutes that I realized that it was not only a prison noir, but a manifesto of disenchantment in the face of power structures. It's a film that rejects the illusion of an “existing” easy redemption; it's a cry of despair against the gears of a system that, by imprisoning bodies, destroys souls. The violence that flows from each scene (physical and psychological) is a reflection of a world ruled by dehumanizing forces, where prison becomes a metaphor for a sick, manipulative and sadistic society.

reviews.author: Kurdt
reviews.text: Another Troubles film, this one a quasi-thriller where a young Catholic who’s IRA-adjacent falls for a new Protestant woman who’s just arrived in town. Here’s the big problem though: he was a key figure in the murder of her husband one year ago. Does a great job capturing how overbearing and constant the violence was, and Cal’s sweet relationship with his father feels especially strong because there’s always a sense that one of them could be ripped away from the other at any time. Also captures how impossible it surely was to just mind your own business and lay low; a side was essentially picked for you by your religion (and the amount of atheists/agnostics in Ireland seems to be incredibly low). It could have gone in a few more intriguing directions towards the end, but still an interesting film.

reviews.text: Mit Calls hat Fede Álvarez ein narratives, audiovisuelles Meisterwerk geschaffen. Die Miniserie erzählt in kurzen Episoden (13 bis 18 Minuten) emotional aufwühlende, unheimliche, mysteriöse Ereignisse zwischen verschiedenen Personen. Erzählt werden die Geschichten über Telefonanrufe und funktionieren quasi wie ein Hörspiel. Visuell wird man lediglich mit den Einblendungen der Namen der Sprecher und Equalizer-artigen Visuals abgeholt. Letztere sind aber so clever an die Geschichten angepasst, dass sie die teils unerträgliche Anspannung perfekt untermalen und sogar noch verstärken. Dazu kommt ein toller Cast, der den Charakteren die Stimmen leiht, wie Aubrey Plaza, Clancy Brown, Karen Gillan, Lily Collins und Pedro Pascal.

Jaggedly edited (or perhaps butchered by its bankrupt producers to salvage a Cable TV premiere) and somewhat nonsensical, it’s mostly interesting just to see Travolta at this crossroads in his career, attempting something “gritty and serious” yet mostly coming off like a concerned guidance counselor in an after-school special. Even moreso given that it's genuinely kind of great, adjusting as needed for the budget and the overall state of the industry in 1981. reviews.text: Initially the rhythm of this was difficult to get a hang of - it's simultaneously repetitive and uneven and wildly unpredictable - but the emotional core reveals itself so gracefully through the vignette structure that it wasn't long before I found myself very moved by each little development. Has all the charm of Takahata's best work, so many incredibly funny moments of visual detail and attention to character (the way each character has their own distinct walk!), and a poignant portrayal of fatherhood that I found personally very affecting. I would say the family trip to the fairground is the highlight were it not for extended cat duel over a stolen testicle.

reviews.author: Daniel
reviews.text: Very sweet and goofy coming of age comedy that is also, typically for Takahata, quietly very sad. Poor old Chie is blissfully unaware of the tragedy in her Mother's concerned expressions and her Father's self destructive behaviour, happily forcing herself into adulthood all too soon. Things work out mostly okay in the end, and the film is hardly miserable; there's far too many funny fighting cats with amusingly prominent testicles, mafia hijinks, and gorgeous 80s Japanese synth music. But like all great films about childhood, the vein of melancholy is why it feels so true in its otherwise innocent silliness.

reviews.text: This was better than most SyFy productions. It’s got some pretty decent special effects, and it has Charles Dance as a demon-looking alien. But it also has way too much characterization. When it comes to many of Arthur C. Clarke’s stories, his characters aren’t there to be related to or feel emotionally connected to… they’re there to move the plot only. To adapt Childhood’s End to the screen and make it palatable to a wider audience, they injected a lot of character development and subplots that didn’t exist in the novel. And this ultimately bogs down what might’ve been a very good adaptation. It spends way too much time on these characters and their lives… resulting in some changes from the novel that hurts this miniseries.

reviews.text: There's a lot to like in this miniseries adaptation of Arthur C. Clarke's science-fiction classic, starting with Charles Dance's performance as a haughty aliens. But there's a lot that's deeply frustrating too, especially as the opening mysteries (what do the aliens want, what do they look like, how will they execute their plan) get answers, and give way to many more mysteries that are never really addressed. By the end of this series, I just had questions, mostly about what was going through the head of any one character. Especially the kids, who were alien enough to be baffling, but not human enough to be interesting. And this series spent waaaaaaaay too much time on two different women who had…

reviews.text: Impressive make-up, good casting and some powerful emotional moments elevate Childhood's End above the average sci-fi television series. It tries hard to hold on to as much of the philosophical trappings of Arthur C. Clarke's novel as it can, but also chooses to give its characters more time on stage in order to give the audience proper closure. While fans of the source material might question some decisions, they cannot deny it has been treated with respect, even if it perhaps could have done with a bit more time to tell its story. Newcomers will find much to like!

reviews.text: With an intimate focus on a community enduring a tragedy, Kinoshita endeavors—perhaps in vain—to photograph the wounds of the soul and spirit. Occupying US forces march through the country, snapping pictures of their destruction. The ruination of Urakami and its people, its buildings and their skin peeled apart by the atomic blast, make for a dramatic picture to send back home to the states. But for those living in the valley before, during, and after the bomb, obviously the damage is much greater, and like the weapon's radioactive output, almost totally invisible. Everything within a mile of ground zero was wiped out, everything for the next mile caught fire, and within and far beyond that, a much deeper sickness takes…

reviews.author: Pretentious Film Critic
reviews.text: Too precise, in the thematic sense, it's about the multiple levels of mourning. It's a requiem for the cadence of daily life and the confidence that tomorrow will arrive. There's this weird "Passion play" in the Stoic monologues. The film wants the audience to reconcile religious belief and direct oppression from the nuclear aftermath. Which makes the movie refuse an easy catharsis. Children of Nagasaki feels deeply personal, and the director refines his themes to harder truths about humanity. I think my problem was that I wanted something more extreme and visceral, not didactic in approach.

reviews.text: It's been a while since I've seen Children of Nagasaki but the lasting effect this film has had on me is astounding. The aftermath of bomb is too much for one person to process and the film makes you understand that. The flash of light and then the quick dissapereance of an entire people. The hurt in the delivery is so impactful. I don't think I've ever cried so hard, if I'm being honest.

reviews.author: Matt Neglia
reviews.text: CHRISTY is a brutal, sobering, and hard-hitting sports biopic that places its emphasis on the painful abuse boxer Christy Martin suffered at the hands of her toxic husband-trainer. It’s an inspirational story that speaks to Christy’s courage and unbreakable determination, both inside the ring and in her fight for survival outside of it. Ben Foster, so effective at playing these despicable characters, rightfully earns the audience’s scorn with a disturbing turn. But the real talking point will be Sydney Sweeney, who delivers the most committed performance of her career thus far in a demanding showcase role, elevating what might have been an otherwise by-the-numbers boxing drama into something far more stirring and impactful.

reviews.text: You could argue that Chuck Wepner, the New Jersey club fighter who miraculously went 15 rounds with heavyweight champion Muhammad Ali, has already had his movie. And he arguably has, as that movie was Rocky; Stallone was working on a spec screenplay about a fighter when he watched Wepner's 1975 bought with Ali. But here, director Philippe Falardeau delivers a genuine biopic of Wepner's life, including his subsequent various meetings with Stallone and his tragicomic attempts to 'be a somebody' in the wake of Oscar winning success.

Schreiber is expectedly great, and is always a delight to see Moss get back to Peggy Olson's shoes, the guys that play Ali and Stallone have a tougher time, specially because the director keeps going for close-ups. As usual for pictures' set in the 70's, the cinematography, production design and soundtrack are excellent.

reviews.author: SnowboardJunkie
reviews.text: You had me at Liev Schreiber plays the original Rocky. The lumbering, loveable punching bag known as the Bayonne Bleeder, Chuck Wepner. The people’s champion of New Jersey who went 15 rounds with Muhammad Ali, quickly proceeded by 15 minutes of fame. But who say’s fame can be good for a man. All the attention lavished on such a big kid at heart only further exonerated him from responsible living. But this is a role Liev was born to play about as much as Ray Donovan and he delivers the goods. If you have an affection for boxing movies, no matter how many get pumped out annually, this is worth a look. One of those stories you find interesting but it doesn’t leave you as a better person afterwards or help you see the world in a new light. Just glutinous entertainment plain and simple.

A24 posting a civil war map––depicting the Western forces, the independent republics, etc.––was meant only to stir up controversy and debate, toying with our expectations. The movie is deliberately vague, giving even less information about the conflict than the map does. I think that’s entirely to its benefit. Civil War is a movie about the aestheticization of war violence. The photojournalists––far from being portrayed as…

reviews.text: Winner of the Grand Jury Prize at the 2019 Sundance Film Festival, Clemency exposes any misconceptions that capital punishment carries any aspects of composure within its contours. Written and directed by Chinonye Chukwu with a comprehensive perspective of a justice system where little improves or changes for the positive despite even the most intense representatives from inside the system attempting to make changes. The films most fascinating aspect is how it's leading star Alfre Woodard (as warden Bernadine Williams) fully demonstrates what her character is thinking and perceiving against the difficulties that Chukwu generates in the warden’s extraordinary responsibilities. Cinematographer Eric Branco contributes some emblematic portraits and Chukwu luminously displays her characters in a variety of different ways. This is a movie which suggests that no matter what position one inhabits within the capital punishment system, the administrative protocols and procedures will invariably take their toll.

The fact that a black woman is at the center as Warden is already something we haven't seen much of before in prison narratives. Additionally, Woodard and Hodge both turn in great performances, and Chukwu's directing is understated but occasionally powerful - the opening sequence is noteworthy, as well as a scene in which Woodard's character coolly recites the execution procedure to Hodge's character.

reviews.author: chavel
reviews.text: A respectful bow to Chinonye Chukwe, the writer/director of Clemency, for taking on the hefty subject of the death penalty without softening it. It should be a very difficult film to get through, but with an assertive shot selection and lean dialogue that strips everything down to its bare essentials, the film envelops you. It opens with an execution gone wrong, and whomever is next in line to die by the mandate of the state should not go through the same torment at time of death. If you’re anti-death penalty, well, nobody should die at all. Especially not an innocent man though who has had new evidence come in that casts a shadow of doubt that he’s guilty at all.…

reviews.author: Bernard Ozarowski
reviews.text: As I left the theater after seeing Clemency, I texted a few friends that the experience of the film was like laying down beneath a cold, wet blanket of unhappiness for two hours. With a few days perspective, the feeling has not changed. It’s a withering, enervating, depressing experience. That isn’t to say the movie isn’t worth your time, it’s an impressive character study. It’s made with a cool, calm precision. Chinonye Chukwu is excellent at putting her actors in a place to succeed. At each moment, I felt the camera and edit perfectly succeeding in capturing the excellent performers. That’s no small feat in a movie mostly made up of scenes of one-on-one dialogue between character pairs.

reviews.text: With Abel Ferrara’s Zeroes and Ones sitting right there, I decided instead to watch this hagiographic documentary about Kevin Smith. Sorry folks, it’s been a hard year and I needed something easy tonight. Anyway, like many white male teenagers of the early- to mid-2000s, I grew up loving Clerks and Chasing Amy before viciously disavowing both them and their maker early in my college years. Now, at age 32, I’ve arrived at the mature, adult position on the issue of Kevin Smith, which is: not a very good filmmaker, but wow, people are still watching Mallrats and maybe that has to count for something. And hey, look at me – I don’t even like his movies, and here I am…

But goodness, I wish they were able to make this a brisk 90 minutes.

reviews.author: anna nomaly
reviews.text: It's impossible for me to look at this from an unbiased perspective, so I won't even attempt to present one. Snowball Effect will likely always remain the quintessential Kevin Smith biography, but this funny and moving deep-dive is a wonderful summary of the man's life, work, and philosophy. Although Malcolm Ingram has been and remains a skilled documentarian, Clerk becomes more than a documentary when—with the exceptions of the new interviews—every anecdote, image, and piece of footage is not only familiar but also has some direct correlation with a period of my own coming-of-age. Hell, Smith's latter-day "be the most me I can be" approach to things is half the reason I started writing capsule reviews again. If my inevitable Clerks III essay winds up having more to do with my personal life than with the film itself, well, don't say I didn't warn you.

reviews.author: Sean Gilman
reviews.text: Exists in this fascinating counter-factual America where Andrew Jackson deals honorably with the Comanche through his emissary Jim Bowie, a romantic soap opera star (Macdonald Carey) and not at all a slave-trading land speculator, to prevent aberrationally greedy Americans (unlike the real Americans, represented by feisty Maureen O'Hara and her wavering Irish accent) from sneaking onto their land to mine their silver. Sherman plays it straight all the way through to the end, with the Comanches triumphant and the future peace assured, with O'Hara and Carey pledging their love (in fact Bowie renounced his American citizenship and became Mexican, complete with wife and family), with only the smallest hint of the real world in the final lines, an allusion to Bowie's part in the Texas Revolution and his death at the Alamo (which he spent in a sick bed, having contracted some mysterious disease). Print the legend.

reviews.text: A couple of admirable starring performances bring life to this HBO original movie (debuting on the network April 16) about the Anita Hill trial: Kerry Washington as Hill, and The Wire's Wendell Pierce as Clarence Thomas. The supporting cast, especially Grace Gummer and Greg Kinnear, is also solid, and the pacing is mostly brisk and tense, except during the press conferences and hearings, which follow the dialogue and pacing of the real-life events, and thus seem stiff and exasperating, just as they did in real life. While the film doesn't solve the mystery of exactly what Thomas said to Washington and when — it portrays both of them as equally grieved and shocked by the other — the narrative here is one I sympathize with, about how Hill's testimony provoked long-lasting political and social change, and outlined a clear divide between men and women about how sexual harassment is interpreted and dismissed.

reviews.text: A truly beautiful movie about a white teacher, Pat Conroy (Jon Voight) sent to a small island community in South Carolina, where his his whole class is made up of black children of various ages. Principal Scott (played the great Madge Sinclair) is very stern and urges Conroy to be the same with the children. But he goes his own way and uses various methods, a lot of them involving fun activities, to reach these kids who have never been taught properly, despite being of Middle School age.

reviews.author: Mattie Lucas
reviews.text: By today's standards, the "white savior" plotline of CONRACK may seem a bit problematic, but what makes the film so interesting is that not only is it based on a true story of a white teacher who takes a substitute job in a rural, all black southern community, it doesn't end with some sort of great triumph. Instead, what he teaches them is to not accept their lot, to demand more, to appreciate their own worth. Whether or not he "saves" them is a point up for debate (the cards remain heavily stacked against them by institutional injustice), but what he does is upend decades of ingrained inferiority in the Jim Crow south. What he gives them is greater than knowledge, it's the knowledge that they are worthy of attention. That's what sets CONRACK apart from the typical inspirational teacher drama, and it's a diamond in the rough.

reviews.author: Fabian
reviews.text: Luchino Visconti's chamber piece Conversation Piece is a one-location drama confined to the rooms of an American aristocrat's palace in Rome. Burt Lancaster plays a retired professor whose peaceful and isolated existence is disturbed by the arrival of a wealthy countess, her younger lover and her daughter along with her boyfriend. The interactions lead to a clash of cultural values, social positions and generational views, as attitudes and opinions are unfolded in a rich, insightful deconstruction of the upper-class bourgeoisie.

reviews.author: Jeremy Milks
reviews.text: My initial reaction was “Holy Shit” after the first 20 minutes. I’ve felt that way about a lot of obscurities that are contenders for the next great vanity project discovery. They can never maintain that rare mystical weirdness that is so hard to describe but truly familiar when you find it. This is a film that goes the whole way. It doesn’t falter or become self-aware at any point. It’s the real deal. A genuine reach for stardom as sincere and convincing as Duke Mitchell in Massacre Mafia Style. Once this gets a proper release, I expect people will freak out when they realize how special this one is.

reviews.author: Joe
reviews.text: I don't try to "objectively" rate movies as much as I try to rate the experience of watching them - that way I don't have to worry about genuinely worthwhile pieces of "outsider art" getting lost in the cracks. As to whether or not Crime Killer qualifies, I have no idea - all I know is it's one of the most bizarre movies I've ever seen, mostly due to the script, pitched somewhere between operatic drama and broken English. The effect of having presumably coherent English-speaking actors delivering this weird gibberish reminded me of The Fountainhead in a weird way.

The scenes involving the family of Steve Thompson (Burt Lancaster) may be necessary to complete his character but, boy, are they deadly. As always, Lancaster is terrific, but the role requires him to do more talking than usual, with a little self-pity, and I prefer Burt…

reviews.text: Deeply beautiful and felt, this biopic of the author Marjorie Kinnan Rawlings of that perennial middle school favorite The Yearling and based partly on her memoir garnered academy award nominations for both Alfre Woodard and Rip Torn in their supporting roles. Its Florida swamp setting is expertly utilized, one of those “the setting is a character” types of films. It’s heartrending and engaging, with humor, and strife, and human connection, and difficult people. There are definite cliches and the like, but the sweeping score (also Oscar nominated) and the care and thought put into it by all the actors and the director tie everything together perfectly. More people need to see this film.

reviews.text: Water and blood, booze and sweat, mud, muck and mire, piss and paint; drowning in a miscible solution of economy, succumbing altogether to the detritic pool of emiction forming at the feet of brigands, mafiosi by necessity, navigating an unyielding existence. Right and wrong replaced with need—no more concepts. Wanting more of this transient life but settling for that which you can put your hands on. How did we get here? It happened in a flash, like that. There seem to be no escape routes. All of those liquids, from the essential to the execrable, have been hosed off rigorously and repeatedly, yet still their spoor remains. Some things can’t be washed away.

It’s a movie that contains imagery that holds a mysterious and dreamlike quality that underlines Hung’s proficiency in visuals, and he crowds each frame with a disturbance of colour and sound. It lays the foundations for some unsettling eye-catching and abstract images of both its locations and characters which congregate into a creative and affecting feast for the eyes.

reviews.author: reibureibu
reviews.text: Colonial territory a negation of its peoples within which finds such people negating its use to the colonizers in negating the land itself. What else can you call its youth planting bombs in their own home? The act of terrorism becomes so unspokenly consigned by the city's own and their latent territorial anger that its outlet becomes those lost children who do not know their own history and do not have their own land and, unlike the older generation with ties to that land, do not care if everything goes in flames. At which point it's less of an ideological stance than it is an existential one, one where the value of life is seen more through its ability to generate the death (the negation) of other lives than in the cultivation of that life itself. No one wins, but at least they lose.

Hark's bullish direction adds a constant sense of escalating momentum to its story of teenage hellions, whose terrorist activities stem from a lack of direction and boredom. Eventually, they fall afoul of a group of American Vietnam War vets whose presence in Hong Kong is wholly ruinous, conjuring still-fresh political wounds of slaughter in Southeast Asia. Doesn't have the revealing outsider thrill of Getty's oddball late-night classic, but makes up for it in sheer commitment to the bit. This totally mishandles mental health, literalizes every metaphor six ways from Sunday, but unlike other movies that try to pretend they have nuance, this takes genuine pride in the ludicrous dumb energy. Everyone is having so much fun with this goofy, sleazy nonsense. Schwarzenegger is ridiculous. I've said before that I prefer this SpectreVision psych-horror freakout type thing to the "elevated" stuff, but if this is how those approaches are bridged, more please.

reviews.author: Sethsreviews
reviews.text: So impressed with this. In all honesty, I’m perplexed by the 3.4 average rating, but I do understand why the measured pacing might not be for everyone. An intimate, heartbreaking, and entirely atmospheric ‘horror’ that hits all the right beats in my opinion. I will say that I am usually very fond of early 2000s/late 90s Japanese horror in general. The cold visual style with a fantastic use of contrast, shadows and practical effects. This is full of grainy voyeuristic shots that completely manage to pull me in. On the surface, this is a horror film about a woman and her daughter moving into a creepy apartment, however, it’s not really a horror film at all. It’s a bleak, sad and tragic drama on grief, isolation and personal crisis. Watched this with my mum from her recommendation and I’m glad I let her pick my 2000th film.

reviews.text: "Day of the Panther" is a 1988 action film directed by Brian Trenchard-Smith. A notable name in the genre of Ozploitation, Trenchard-Smith has a slew of novelty titles to his name. "Day of the Panther" fits in amongst is other native Australian venues such as "Stunt Rock" (1978), "Turkey Shoot" (1982) and "Dead End Drive-In" (1988) to name a few. From this translated energy, he then made his way into the Hollywood system, majority of his work being direct to video efforts, including some sequels within the "Leprechaun" (1993) series, specifically "Leprechaun 3: In Vegas" (1995) and "Leprechaun 4: In Space" (1996), as well as "Night of the Demons 2" (1994) as a follow up within that series.

reviews.author: belial_carboni
reviews.text: Another unearthed 80s slasher from Jose Larraz that really hit the spot. While not as visceral, jarring or unique as Edge of the Axe Deadly Manor still has a lot going for it. While it is a little slower and goofier it also has funnier characters, more sleaze and lots of unintentional humor. Add in a creepy haunted house setting, late 80s synth magic and sprinkles of gore Deadly Manor comes together as a solid mid tier slasher.

reviews.author: Sofa Sinema
reviews.text: When this started I was getting major Lynchian vibes, especially after seeing those dark majestic woods, a hooting owl, naked corpses, and a truck with a giant Bob's Big Boy winding around a lonely lost highway. There's a decent mystery element here with languid and eerily erotic scenes. The characters are a mixed bag of the obvious and most contrived genre staples, but spending time sneaking around this strange manor with this oddly mellow group mostly worked for me. The final act has more standard slasher elements, but it retains an offbeat creepiness with its dark and shadowy setting that comes across exquisitely in Arrow's HD presentation.

reviews.author: Aberrant Ghoul
reviews.text: This was a standard but kinda ok 80s slasher (even if it was released in 1990). Sure, it's a little light on the gore and too many kills happen off-camera, but the setting wins it a lot of bonus points, having been filmed on location at a derelict 100-year-old mansion that was scheduled for demolition. I mean, what else is there to say about this? The plot is the most derivative Horror 101 nonsense. Some teens spend the night in a creepy, dilapidated house after picking up a shady-looking hitchhiker. What could possibly go wrong?

reviews.author: Slig001
reviews.text: For this film, director José Ramón Larraz decided to make a largely rather dull slasher. The film follows on from the common trope of a bunch of young kids caught together in a place where a killer is on the loose. Fans of Larraz will likely be disappointed with this one. There's none of the sexuality or intrigue that made the likes of Vampyres, Whirlpool and Symptoms such classics. The film takes place in a remote woodland setting but that's about it for comparisons to Larraz's earlier works. There's no real atmosphere and a surprising lack of tension, making the vast bulk of the film really boring. There's a fairly high body count but the murders are all rather bland.…

reviews.author: MushiMinion
reviews.text: A real wet fart of a slasher that takes 'slow burn horror' to a whole new level. Nothing even happens in Deadly Manor until an hour into it, and all you're rewarded with is swift, bloodless kills whose imagination caps out at, "hand holding knife appears from off camera, stabs person." I've never seen hunting to be a sign of good character in thrillers, e.g. Silvio Amadio's Amuck! and Larraz's own The Coming of Sin, and this is no exception. The man's house is practically covered with animal trophies. My love Rosalba Neri is in this for less than five minutes (and even that's generously counting) as an Indian woman whom he's "forced to do things that no woman would have accepted". reviews.text: José Ramón Larraz tepid horror about a remarried Englishman in India who has been cursed by his former servent/lover. Antonio Molino Rojo, Mary Maude and Raffaele Curi star along with a cameo by Rosalba Neri as the servant. Like most of Larraz's films it's slow moving but uncharacteristically fails to capitalize on the sleazy aspects of the story and has little in the way of atmosphere. The tiger/woman stalking was a good idea but the direction and editing of the scenes came up short. There is a surprising ending and the film isn't a total washout but far from Vampyres, Symptoms or even The House That Vanished.

reviews.text: This slow paced gothic mystery wasn't the first film by Jose Larraz that I wanted to experience, but it popped up on YouTube and appears to be a bit of a rarity so I wanted to catch it in case it got taken down.A plantation owner in India scorns a lover who puts a curse on him before committing suicide. When he remarries he starts to doubt his sanity, believing his lover is back to haunt him, symbolised by a roaming tiger in the jungle.Despite its languid pace I quite enjoyed this. It had a decent amount of atmosphere going for it and was stylish in places. Had all the trappings of a gothic romance. The print of the film was terrible though. Faded and scratched almost throughout. Would be good if this got a proper restoration as it apparently hadn't even been released on VHS.

reviews.author: Joe
reviews.text: Aesthetics (or my rating) can't explain the weird attachment I feel for this movie. It might be attributed to pure sentiment on my part, but instead I think it's the unaccountably light atmosphere of imagination that's mostly to blame. Despite the sometimes chintzy CGI and digital cinematography, I always feel caught up in this wave of fantasy in a way that I almost never do with other comparable blockbusters. Not even the ones that are straight-up better movies (with better endings, not that that's saying much in this case) - I might be more gripped by them, but this one offers a distinct kind of pleasure.

reviews.text: Based on famed Tang Dynasty chancellor Di Renjie and the fictionally novelized recounting of his life titled Dee Goong An or ‘Cases of Judge Dee’ (18th century), Tsui Hark’s Detective Dee and the Mystery of the Phantom Flame (2010) goes big in an attempt to separate itself from decades of television shows that share its blend of 7th century historical characters and events, crime investigation, and paranormal mystery with a noteworthy cast and an emphasis on both art direction and fight choreography.

reviews.author: Jake Cole
reviews.text: Sammo Hung's intricate slapstick combat meets Tsui's buoyant visual energy and the undercurrent of commentary beneath. For all the goofy energy of this caper, we're still left with the grim sense that Dee goes to such lengths to absolve and protect a transparent autocrat whose harsh rule will make life miserable for many. Tsui shoots the grandeur of imperial China both to establish the playgrounds for his action and to highlight the vast, ungodly wealth of the system Dee works to maintain out of social impetus and loyalty.

reviews.author: Filipe Furtado
reviews.text: More imaginative, more wild. Part of what sets the Dee movies apart is how Tsui notions of fantasy include a good deal of horror and this offers many examples of that. His eye for aggressive fake CG remains very good. The mix of weird Chinese fantasy, supernatural mystery and political intrigue is probably the most balanced in the series so far, even if the plot feels looser. As these films progresses so does the ambivalence towards Dee’s position as keeper of autocratic regime he is suspicious at best. Also, Carina Lau’s Empress Wu remain one of the decade’s best and most relevant creations.

reviews.author: sydney
reviews.text: sometimes you hear dorks throw out that "the bad CGI really took me out of the movie" bullshit, and i couldn't stop thinking about that because the exact opposite was true of this movie. obviously none of it is real, but the costumes + set designs + actors were all so good that i couldn't imagine any of it existing outside of the movie, couldn't comprehend that everyone would check email on their phone between takes and then go back to normal modern life. can't express how desperately i wish big budget hollywood directors would embrace the fact that CGI is never going to look real, and fill their movies with flying blades and giant palaces and impossible stunts and magic folktale monsters.

reviews.text: The third of Tsui Hark’s Detective Dee films, is a significant departure from the previous entries. While action films in the vein of Guy Richie’s Sherlock Holmes, they are grounded in supernatural mysteries that usually have realistic solutions. The Robert Downey Jr. Hound of the Baskervilles that will smash box office records if they can ever get around the problem of Holmes barely being in it. The mystery is never that deep but they are there - most prominently in the first film, Phantom Flame. Sea Dragon had substantially more fantasy elements and large action set pieces, but there were still crimes to deduce. With Four Heavenly Kings, the mystery is more simple, used to explain monstrous visuals that might…

reviews.text: magnificent. I want to say the best of the Dee's, but I haven't seen the others since their initial release. I know I didn't love any of them this much tho. this film has such movement, near-constant mutation yet with sudden bursts into different mental states, moods, tensions, and realities. from crowded streets new planes of existence unravel in the mist. the ending's emotional registers recalled King Hu's Buddhist films, and the Hong Kong cop elements move with the grace of Tsui Hark's late 80s and mid 90s works (of what I've seen).

reviews.text: The Detective Dee films owe a lot to the Star Wars Prequels and the Matrix movies when it comes to the implementation of digital and the use of CGI in the action scenes. Those films, in turn, owe a lot to classic wuxia and martial arts films when it comes to their archetypal storytelling, their compositions, and the blend of kineticism and grace in their action scenes. Just a great example of cinema learning from its past and paving the way for the future. Great artists expressing their gratitude to each other through their art.

See also, BlackCandles, Symptoms and Vampyres if you like this as much as me. Larraz was very good at catching that brief period in England when it seemed that little rich kids could do just about anything they wanted. And what a lot wanted to do was sex and drugs and play with the paranormal. In this instance we start out with a tale of taxidermy but somehow that gets forgotten and we have a more usual tale of pretty suburban girl lured into posh kids den of iniquity. Lisbet Lundquist is stunning as the vampire like lady…

It kicks off when Olivia & Paul, a couple heading out of London for a dirty weekend, accidentally run over and kill a pedestrian in the woods, putting their car out of action in the process. They're given shelter by a brother and sister who live in a large country house, and it becomes clear that even though the accident victim was one of their friends, they don't want the police involved and don't hold…

reviews.text: Wonderfully moody piece about an unfaithful bloke, Paul (Malcolm Terris) and his girlfriend Rebecca (Sibyla Grey) who end up crashing their car on woodlands back roads. Luckily for them, they are "rescued" by siblings Julian (Karl Lanchbury) and Olivia (Lisbeth Lundquist) - much of the same cast as in Larraz previous erotic thriller Whirlpool in 1970.

reviews.author: BodyBoy
reviews.text: I like the look of Larraz's second feature, the darkness and the hippie sex conundrum that crutches the picture... but I found it hard to care or pay attention. Shame too - many unique plot choices and in some ways expands on the limits of Whirlpool and predicts both the murderous ways of his future films as well as the odd airs of House That Vanished and Estigma but during the more 'precious' moments like the flower by the water, I noticed a lack of strength. It's hard to say how much of an auteur Larraz is even 7 or 8 films in, but I know when somebody isn't putting their all into a concept that should be embraced. Maybe a cleaned up print would sway me higher, but I found the sepia to be a nice touch.

reviews.text: I really adore this period in Italian genre cinema. Gory horror flicks were slowly being discarded in favour of glamorous thrillers. Less interested in delivering brutal kills/gore and more focussed on creating an aesthetically pleasing experience full of atmosphere. I'm thinking of movies like Too Beautiful to Die, Body Puzzle and (to a lesser extend) Arabella: Black Angel. Ruggero Deodato's Dial: Help is definitely part of that tradition. The set-up is pretty out there, but it's also a lot of fun. A perfect movie for a lazy afternoon.

Они представили сюжет не о типичном подвиге, где бравый боец стремится к победе над злодеем, как в Алёше Поповиче. Добрыня Никитич попадает в запутанную ситуацию, устроенную сразу несколькими неоднозначным персонажами. Главная его цель - выяснить правду и убедиться, что старый друг таковым остаётся. Он живёт приключениями, но не упивается собственной силой и достижениями. Очередное боевое задание для него не более, чем способ укрыться от обыденной семейной рутины. А в качестве награды устроит любая вещь, позволяющая заткнуть жену на пару дней.Примечательной деталью является то, что все участники истории, встающие на пути Добрыни или сбивающие с него, мотивированы…

Unlike Yuen Woo-ping's films with Chan in Snake in the Eagle's Shadow or Drunken Master, it's also completely devoid of slapstick humour and is a mostly straight-laced action film with a very basic plot and characters, making it virtually indistinguishable from many other low-budget Hong Kong martial arts movies of its time. reviews.text: Ostensibly an ideal paring of Moon Lee and Oshima Yukari, who dueled so memorably in Teresa Woo’s Iron Angels, but ultimately stolen by Sibelle Hu. They play two women who have been raised since childhood by Eddy Ko to be the perfect assassins. Moon starts to feel some human emotions when one of their hits incinerates a van-full of children, but things really go wrong on a mission to Thailand, where Moon gets knocked unconscious and catches a nasty case of amnesia. This is where the other part of the film, which has actually taken up most of the running time, becomes relevant.

A world with no sentiment where almost anyone can get hurt in crime. Blurry yet cohesively messy. Lo-fi action cinema with so much heart and charisma. Glorious. The meaning of the dreams are earned, no matter the forms they take in reality.

reviews.author: Robert Daniels
reviews.text: From the moment Carol (Elizabeth Banks) allows a lookalike android to enter her home, DreamQuil wears its influences on its sleeve. A mix of Stepford Wives, Rear Window and Rosemary’s Baby, the high-concept sci-fi finds Carol unmoored in her marriage with Gary (John C. Reilly) and as a mother to Quentin (Toby Larsen). So, she turns to the people at DreamQuil, who promise an immersive therapy that will help her reclaim herself. It’s a decision that will flip this dystopian high-concept sci-fi into a harried psychological thriller, whose enthralling style is not enough to overcome its cliched storytelling. [full review via Screen Daily]

reviews.author: Ben Hibburd
reviews.text: Of all the late 80s/early 90s action stars, Wesley Snipes was by far the most underappreciated. The guy was just as charismatic as Arnie; he had the moves that could complement JCVD and Dolph Lundgren, and he could actually carry a film with real acting talent, unlike the others mentioned. And whilst he might not of had the best scripts, he sure made the most out of them. Take "Drop Zone" for example, this film is essentially a complete rip off of "Point Break", and it could've easily felt like a cheap direct-to-TV cash-in. Snipes, however, lends this film enough credibility to make it a highly enjoyable B-movie, and I mean that in the best possible way.

reviews.text: Drop Zone is a 1994 film directed by John Badham. Starring Wesley Snipes in the central role, the film is a action thriller that mainly uses the influence of skydiving as its narrative booster. Snipes plays U.S. Marshal Pete Nessip who was facilitating the transport of a high-profile computer hacker prisoner with his brother Terry, also a U.S. Marshal. In the most uncanny of manners, a prison break heist is facilitated on board the plane of transport. With little to go on but knowing that the hijackers were skilled in skydiving, this is where Pete (who has now gone a bit rogue) begins his search to find the assailants.

reviews.text: The nineties represented the high-water mark for mainstream skydiving interest. The World Free Fall Convention began in 1990, running throughout the decade and a little beyond, before finally until winding down in 2006. ESPN made the extreme sport a big part of their X Games, at least initially. By the time Point Break came out in 1991, Hollywood was eager to get in on the action and put a number of films in theaters featuring or revolving around skydiving. None of them would hit the heights of Kathyrn Bigelow’s iconic film, but movies like Terminal Velocity and Honeymoon in Vegas (flying Elvi!!) made for a fun night at the movies. reviews.text: Grossly irresponsible to make a film that attempts to examine the intensely vitriolic state of American politics amidst the earliest months of COVID and not mention how Trump, or the MAGA-sphere, directly amplified and exacerbated so many of those very issues. But at least we can laugh about the youths caring very loudly about George Floyd’s murder. And we can roll our eyes at the women who succumb to right-wing conspiracies as a coping mechanism to deal with trauma that exists just to make them difficult to stomach. I found every part of this uninteresting and, maybe even worse, unintelligent. No interest in digging into the nuances that exist within this reality, no attempt at reconciling with these experiences, just nonstop upping the ante in the bizarrely cruel and misguided ways Aster seems to be gravitating towards more with each new film.

Aster makes a film that unsparingly aims to render what it feels like to be alive in the present, which is to say a baffling experience mediated entirely by screens that produces total alienation. What this movie does better than anything is portray this ubiquitous sense that there is some unspecified DOOM out there with our names written on it. It it the virus or is it the cure? Regardless of your politics everyone has some version of this, and we're all convinced that everyone else is lying to us about the nature of this…

reviews.author: Sam
reviews.text: This is such a great drama and one which is very thought-provoking and honestly, kind of shocking even today. It takes a hard look into religious showmanship in early 20th-century America and critiques the institution but never mocks real faith. It was obviously shocking when it came out due to how religion is portrayed through charisma and spectacle for profit. There's an intriguing line between performance and belief which asks strong moral questions but doesn't offer easy answers. I also think this is one of my favorite Lancaster performances and one for which he deserved the awards he got since it's so fast-talking and electric and just so multi-layered it's hard not to love every second. Overall, the core ideas this one explores are ridiculously intriguing and it's a film which makes you really sit and think where you stand on its morals, but it always remains slightly theatrical in execution while anchored by powerhouse performances.

reviews.author: laird
reviews.text: The Stand By Me of triad films. I'm glad I watched The Mission within the last month, because it really gave Exiled a "we're getting the old band back together" feel. I love watching these guys together, and clearly they love working together (and with To). So much is communicated in their glances and gestures to one another. While seemingly every major action director was still dragging out Matrix "bullet time" and stale 90s Hong Kong tricks, To is constantly experimenting and innovating with how to stage and film a shootout. Here billowing curtains, tarps, and misty blood add kineticism to the typically tense and tight fixed location gun play. It's extremely exciting, quirky, and funny, as I've come to expect from To, but unlike any of his other movies I've seen, I found this one genuinely moving (as opposed to just rousing, if that makes sense). Maybe that's just the cold medicine talking, I don't know.

reviews.author: comrade_yui
reviews.text: an intimate ode to blood-soaked brotherhood, johnnie to's spiritual sequel to his masterpiece the mission channels his existential melancholia into a florid elegy for camaraderie and the emotional weight of violence. the mission itself was stylized as an impish, intelligent purification of the heroic bloodshed genre, stripping every histrionic explosion of violence down into an ice-cold standoff between the professional respect & kinship of killers and the ritualistic expectations of their underworld society. exiled unravels every bit of lighthearted gloss from its predecessor, charting the complete tragic and inevitable destruction of a hitman fellowship that would never be able to realistically achieve their private dreams of normalcy and peace.

reviews.author: Angelica Jade Bastién🪼🌷
reviews.text: Sterling example of dudes fucking rock cinema. An action flick that’s surprisingly sweet natured given the camaraderie amongst its main group of gangster assassins. This is a film with Red Bull in its veins. This is a world where everything especially the virtuosic gun play is poetic. Those sequences of gun fights are utterly delectable. That opening sequence which starts with tension, devolves into operatic gun play, and then turns into a friendly romp where both groups of underworld figures end up helping the ex-gangster dude and his new family move their furniture into their new abode. Such intriguing visual language — beyond but including the gun play. The settings — how they’re framed, utilized, dressed and lit — to create such rich physical spaces to juxtapose against the violence; baby this is cinema! A bloody, pitch-perfectly embodied, violent, fun affair I will be thinking about for a long time. Movies should always be this cool.

reviews.author: mumon
reviews.text: Farewell Amor (2020) is about an Angolan family of three reuniting in the US after the father had been living there for almost two decades on his own. The Q&A with director Ekwa Msangi (that MUBI showed after the stream) revealed that the premise is based on relatives of her and serves as a what if scenario for them (her uncle went to the US with a student visa but was repeatedly denied the immigration of his family). Although necessarily touching upon it, the movie is not primarily about the immigrant experience, but rather about the toll separation, exile, and living in different societies over a long time takes on our personal relationships.

reviews.author: Mitchell Smoothy
reviews.text: Marc Abraham’s Flash of Genius is an earnest and thought-provoking drama that highlights the power of perseverance and the personal toll of fighting for justice, based on the true story of Robert Kearns, the inventor of the intermittent windshield wiper, who waged a decades-long legal battle against major automakers that had infringed on his patent. Greg Kinnear delivers a heartfelt performance as Kearns, capturing his unwavering determination and the emotional strain of his quest for recognition. Kinnear’s portrayal is grounded and compelling, effectively portraying the sacrifices Kearns made to defend his principles, even as his relentless pursuit alienated his family and strained his health.

The post-apocalyptic setting for example reminded me a lot of Nausicaä of the Valley of the Wind while the two leads, Conan and Lana,…

reviews.text: Aesthetics, adventure, values​​... most of Miyazaki's poetics are present. One big difference from future works is that there are some real villains to contend with here. There is a bit of naivety, a couple of characters have a weird or hasty arc; the plot instead is well orchestrated and always entertaining. Over the course of the series the overall quality progressively improves and as we approach the finale everything becomes more dramatic and spectacular. In the last third the animation reaches very high peaks, a display of techniques that are still of great impact.

reviews.author: Darren Carver-Balsiger
reviews.text: A pleasant little anime film by the masterful Isao Takahata, Gauche the Cellist is very childish, but also very sweet. It's a simple story of a lacklustre musician who gets four important lessons from some talking animals to help him improve, albeit unknowingly. It's not very complex and perhaps, detrimentally, without purpose. Having said that, it tells its story in a perfectly fine manner. The animation has some beautiful moments but it's rather flat and unimaginative, although as this is pre-Ghibli it had a lot less budget. By far the most wonderful thing though is the use of classical music, which plays almost constantly at times, transitioning scenes as well as playing over them or being a part of the plot. Overall, Gauche the Cellist is an enjoyable romp which executes its story well even if it rarely astonishes.

reviews.text: A gorgeous lie. This isn’t a documentary: every shot is clean, every conversation suspiciously in service to a narrative. Using non-professional actors doesn’t make it non-fiction. This is at best way over-directed; at worst scripted. The filmmakers—none of whom are Argentinian, if that matters to you—have made a beautiful, probably well-intentioned portrait of Argentinian cowboy culture and the young woman who wants to break into it. The people we see may be authentic, but this film sure ain’t.

reviews.author: Matt Neglia
reviews.text: GAUCHO GAUCHO is an observant, stunningly gorgeous-looking examination of Argentine cowboys and cowgirls from the directors of The Truffle Hunters. Its cinematic allure is so captivating I found myself forgetting more than once it was even a documentary. Every frame of this black & white slice of life film is flawless featuring the best cinematography of the festival, while the sound design is completely immersive backed by a terrific soundtrack. Yet, beyond its technical artistry, I yearned for a deeper connection to its slice-of-life presentation.

reviews.author: claira curtis
reviews.text: Often feels more like a narrative than a documentary thanks to how it interweaves scenes of its subjects. Gaucho Gaucho’s ability to focus itself on Gauchos from all generations allows us to see essentially the full life of those who are a part of the community and how much similarity and difference can be found in their perspectives. Cinematography is breathtaking and all the more powerful thanks to its black & white grading. A quiet, but firm reminder that we are outsiders looking in briefly on a life we will never truly experience. We can never see these moments in their full context or color and that only makes what the film does encompass all the more special.

reviews.author: Lucinda
reviews.text: Feels even more staged than your average Sundance-style documentary, and is extremely light on actual info, failing to answer many of the questions that even the most idly curious viewer probably has. How big is the town where these people live and what does it look like – are there modern shops and houses there, or cars? How much of the gaucho lifestyle do people actually lead or is it just something that happens around their more conventional lives? What do they all do for a living? How big are these rodeo events that they have, how often do they occur, and to what extent is the community involved in putting them on?

reviews.author: Ella Kemp
reviews.text: Very happy to now be able to say: I love this film! It is beautiful, moving, fleeting, poetic. It is a film about community, and pays respect to all the greatest parts of cinema history that came before it.

reviews.author: BrandonHabes
reviews.text: Less of a documentary and more of a carefully manicured visual poem that almost fooled me for a cinematic fiction. Perhaps that’s the real mystery of this highly stylized, observational feast—not knowing whether it succeeds as a romantic love letter to a vanishing way of life or fails as a performative smokescreen that leans far too much into its mythmaking and aestheticizing impulses to really glean the interiority of its subjects. Somewhere on that razor’s edge a vérité dance takes shape, striking a blend between artifice and actuality distilled into a pure cinematic language that wants to immortalize a deep and proud tradition, but perhaps can only get there with skin deep perspective.

reviews.text: Acts as both a critique of the Hollywood system and a study of the trauma and danger that lies within open homosexuality. It’s incredibly rare - hell, I can’t think of another American queer film - that is written, directed, and stars an actual gay person, so it’s surprisingly refreshing that there’s one from the 90s. Ian McKellen delivers his finest performance as the retired classic director James Whale, showcasing a stunning amalgamation of the emotional intensities and delicacies that come with age and sexuality. While this may seem like a shock, and it could be a personal matter, but I doubt I’ve ever seen homosexuality portrayed this well on film with regard to the mentality and mannerisms of this character, making Gods and Monsters as special as it is.

At the heart of Bill Condon’s brilliant, semi-fictionalized recounting of James Whale’s (Ian McKellen) final days is the budding but fraught friendship that develops between Whale and his new gardener, Clay Boone (Brendan Fraser). It’s a friendship explicitly and lovingly framed through the gothic lens of “Frankenstein” motifs, with Whale and Boone cycling between the identities of Dr. Frankenstein and the Creature he creates. Whale, the artist and former director, is a man haunted by and consumed with his past—a past replete with impoverished, working-class origins, familial rejection, and love lost in the horrors of the Great War. reviews.text: An early prototype for the intersecting, multiple character plot. Here, it’s five different people staying at the Grand Hotel in Berlin - a baron, a ballerina, a stenographer, a dying man and a businessman - who all cross paths in one way or another. The film was publicized as the “battle of the stars” and director Edmund Goulding was nicknamed the “lion tamer” because of the number of high profile actors: Greta Garbo, John Barrymore, Lionel Barrymore, Wallace Beery, Joan Crawford and Lewis Stone. It’s such a treat to see these great actors work together, and the simple plot is surprisingly compelling. Plus, you get to hear Garbo say “I vant to be alone...”

The film's social critique broadens when two snake spirits take the form of radically different women. One attempts to assimilate, falling in love and even getting pregnant, the latter detail used as the ultimate proof of her humanity and worth. reviews.text: Had a great conversation with Wafflez on how the obsession of reading each piece of media one consumes with the same particular lens prevents one from taking in anything new, instead repurposing all stories to be in service of one's individual experience while ignoring any other purpose. There is nothing wrong with finding relatability within media but a singular approach ends up telling less about the work itself than the one who approaches it, and especially when applied to the works of cultures / communities outside one's own does this become destructive: such singularity "mines" a work specifically to look for one element out of the whole but in doing so it also "under-mines" past everything else, destroying everything else.…

reviews.author: reibureibu
reviews.text: Understands that wuxia at its heart is steeped in romance, that one cannot have the former without the latter and as such the romance must not be neglected in favor of action. Indeed romance itself is a term of action, the courting and flirtations as much a battle of wills as is a clashing of fist and feet and which certainly leads to a sparring of bodies. Here Hark pays as much attention to this romantic sparring, the motion of those in love and their lovemaking as concentrated and choreographed as the actual action scenes, and even those germinate from the seeds of romance as all conflict within revolve around love.

reviews.text: for tsui hark, the truth of his fantasy worlds is not the moment in which all the shadows shrouding the world disappear (under some crystalline clarity of either the buddhist's ascetic haughtiness or the taoist's self-righteous academic pursuit), but rather as the moment of eclipse: not the unity of all things embraced by rationalistic solar light, but the destruction of subjectivity that creates pure individuation, when 'one turns into two', when the moon meets the sun and their polarity is accentuated to the maximum extent, when divine unity is destroyed and a whole world of difference is fragmented into a million shades of color & contrast. only by working within these contrasts, not as an agent of 'balance' or equilibrium, but through embracing the fallibility and doubt of our engagement. value is only found through this perception, life begins in the mixed shadows of diffused existence, not in the sterile blinding truth of abstracted divine order.

reviews.text: For how much Green Zone feels like an attempt by Paul Greengrass and Matt Damon to capture the same style of the Bourne films, it's still a pretty solid war film which approaches the Iraq War in a fairly scathing way. It's an angry film, for sure, and it doesn't pull too many punches when it comes to how it eviscerates the US' actions in the conflict. At the same time, it's also a tightly-paced, propulsive action film where the action is a lot more realistic than the duo's previous work. It does have the same shakycam that their Bourne movies are criticized for, but that style fits with Green Zone in how it depicts the intensity of warfare as both an action movie and as an indictment of events in Iraq.

We follows several cars' occupants - the obligatory pregnant woman, the band thinking of breaking up, etc. - and John Beck as a heroic traffic expert at headquarters who might be able to get things moving again, if only his boss would listen to his ideas. Played as a gentle comedy, Gridlock is inoffensive but watchable, a very light spoof of disaster movies with its own story to tell.
