reviews.text: Long-unseen footage from Clouzot's lost masterpiece, the unfinished L'enfer (1964), is brought back to life through the efforts of director Serge Bromberg, who came across the subject after being trapped in an elevator with Clouzot's widow. The incredible footage is a gift to cinema, though the documentary that frames it is not without faults. It does a fine job of illustrating the breakdown of the production, framing Clouzot as a director who, like his American counterpart Hitchcock, employed careful planning, storyboards and clockwork precision. But when Clouzot finally receives the attention of Hollywood and is given carte blanche, he becomes lost in his own obsession for perfection; shooting and reshooting scenes that were already in the can and putting his…

reviews.author: Allison M. 🌱
reviews.text: First viewing: April 2010First review:Amazing film about the madness of a director. Henri-Georges Clouzot was making the film and had an unlimited budget, an excellent crew, and top actors, yet the film still went completely wrong and was never released. Serge Bromberg takes the original footage, goes behind the scenes and has actors Jacques Gamblin and Bérénice Bejo act out unfilmed scenes straight from the script. Since I have a keen interest in Clouzot's work, I was thrilled to see this film. However, if you'd like to know more about this adventurous director who pushed the limits of cinema and was a true auteur, I would suggest you check it out.

reviews.author: Frankco Lamerikx
reviews.text: Mislabeled here on Letterboxd, because this documentary about the making of Henri-Georges Clouzot's unfinished 1964 film L'enfer was made in 2009, and is a film on its own. Yes, it contains a lot of footage from the original film, but it is first and foremost a documentary on how the film came about, the wild ideas that Clouzot had on how to portray the mental state of his protagonist, how he received carte blanche from the American producers, how he got entangled in his own perfectionism, and how the film finally had to be abandoned after the lead actor left, his replacement walked off the set after four days, and Clouzot himself suffered a cardiac episode.

reviews.text: The incredible images Clouzot and his camera crews were able to create in real time, without the advent of digital effects, are staggering in their hallucinatory inventiveness. They were, quite simply, on the vanguard of experimental film. I don't know if he could have pulled off their integration in to the fiction film he envisioned, especially given the conditions of the production, but seeing the germination of these ideas gives me chills and leaves me with a bittersweet longing.

reviews.author: Joe Wawrzyniak
reviews.text: This particular A&C vehicle is pretty lightweight, but still often amusing just the same. The central story concerning a bank robbery is kind of disjointed, but fortunately there's more than enough choice A&C tomfoolery to compensate for the admittedly flimsy narrative. Amongst the sidesplitting comic highlights are Lou Costello pretending to play the piano, Lou wreaking hilarious havoc while trying and failing to ice skate, and the positively hysterical slapstick skiing climax that comes complete with a funny cameo from a guy in a bear suit. The teller verbal routine rates as a truly inspired rib-tickling moment. Ginny Simms provides oodles of spunky spark as a sultry singer. Elyse Knox likewise enchants as a perky nurse. Johnny Long and His Orchestra perform several charming musical numbers. Moreover, it's always a treat to see veteran villainous character dude Marc Lawrence cast to type in one of his patented flunky roles. An enjoyably cheery'n'frothy romp.

reviews.text: Poverty Row wartime exploitation flick directed by Nick Grinde, with an awesome premise to excite any fan of vintage trash. An American businessman puts a price on Hitler's head — a million dollars, dead or alive. The takers are three gangsters of the Prohibition era who were just released from Alcatraz, headed by Ward Bond, in a rare lead role. Unhinged from commitment to realism or good taste, the film's cheapness grants it a freedom to relish absurdities, with heroes who drink while they drive and whose master plan for infiltrating Germany is... to speak English in American accents and hope it works out. What's enjoyable here is that the film takes place in a world where our heroes' plans (almost) always work out, a world where Nazi officials conveniently communicate exclusively in English and where three Joe Blows can not only take Hitler but can have fun while doing it.

reviews.author: Curtis
reviews.text: Rafe Stoker (William Smith) is a B-movie actor who wants to make, with his girlfriend Julie (Mary Woronov), his own bikesploitation classic, but lacks the funds. Desperate to bring his vision to the screen, he makes a deal with Angelo (Angelo Farese), a mobster who throws some cash at Stoker, but with the very explicit instructions that the movie must be complete, in one month, or Angelo's organization gets everything Stoker has. And to guarantee that Stoker doesn't meet his deadline, Angelo's crew hires a group of bikers led by Harvey (Ray Girardin) to act as...disrupters. Plus, the local Floridian law doesn't take too kindly to those Hollywood types.

reviews.author: Justin LaLiberty
reviews.text: In the same year that saw Mel Brooks' Silent Movie and Elia Kazan's The Last Tycoon, we got perhaps the most honest movie about filmmaking we could get with Jack Starrett's exploitative crime drama featuring the mafia taking on the director of a biker movie. Its as salacious and conventional as you'd expect from a 70s Starrett feature, but it also has about as much to say about the art of movie-making as Day for Night and approaches the business end with about as much mirth and trepidation as The Nice Guys did forty years later.

Also a rare turn for Mary Woronov as a romantic lead. Feels like a cheaper companion piece to something like the Robert Forster movie Stunts. This one was a real surprise.

reviews.author: Darren Carver-Balsiger
reviews.text: Horus, Prince of the Sun [or The Little Norse Prince] is one of the most important anime films of all time. Not only did it set a new standard for anime cinema, it was the film that debuted and cemented the collaboration of Isao Takahata and Hayao Miyazaki, who in turn created anime's finest films. Although this is Isao Takahata's directorial debut, it seems very much like a Miyazaki film. There is fantasy and a non-Japanese visual influence, both Miyazaki hallmarks, and Miyazaki's Nausicaa and the Valley of the Wind seems to borrow visuals and plot elements from Horus, Prince of the Sun. reviews.text: Unlike most projects suffering heavy studio interference, the hellish production Isao Takahata's directorial debut went through just makes me embrace the end result even more. The workers' unionization themes arguably wouldn't have developed as strongly, nor resonated as clearly, had Takahata, Hayao Miyazaki, et al., been given total creative freedom. Significant losses in their battle against Toei's execs included reducing the running time by over half an hour, and swapping indigenous Ainu people (whose legend inspired the puppet show this fable originated from) for vaguely Scandinavian to avoid controversy. Like the socialist subtext, the intended setting becomes blatantly obvious once you're made aware of it. Sure, the two unfinished action scenes sting (time and money ran out), but they're situated…

reviews.author: Anastasia
reviews.text: So underrated, I missed old animations like this. Long before Studio Ghibli was formed, Isao Takahata and Hayao Miyazaki had already worked on several projects, and this was their first major collaboration. It set a new standard for anime cinema, and the visuals are stunning. It definitely deserves more recognition the story is amazing. I love all of their early work. I remember being so surprised by Hilda’s "truth" she is such a complex character. When Horus found out, he didn’t abandon her, he just kept asking her to return and helped her find her way back. The village vibes are so wholesome, and while it follows a classic rescue trope, it has so much more depth. Overall, Horus: Prince of the Sun is a sweet, short fantasy film that remains a masterpiece of anime history. It’s great for kids, and even years later, I remember exactly how much of an effect it had on me.

reviews.text: This is a reserved, quiet explication of the anarchic ideas of Zero for Conduct with a core of sorrow. It's astonishing how elegantly this film depicts coming-of-age disillusionment, acknowledges the futility of (being born?) a life in such a world, and still retain a certain feeling of child-like joy in the wide open world. There's more than one shot where both brothers do the same thing, one brother slightly behind the other, walking along in unison, and every time it happened, I just felt my brain bleed in some sort of twisted delight at the visual, even when it was a sad one.

reviews.author: BrandonHabes
reviews.text: I was born, but then I grew up and learned that hero worship is a bitch of a thing. I was born, but then I grew up and discovered that real power is not acquired by what I learned on the playground and schoolyards. Power and hero worship are the twin pillars of Ozu's domestic, coming-of-age, cross-examining tale between old and young generations. Keiji and Ryoichi, two young brothers bullied by a gang of neighborhood kids, have a very specific image of how power is gained.

reviews.text: One of the funniest silent comedies, and also one of the hardest-hitting as it completes the shift Tokyo Circus signaled from Lloyd to Chaplin. The camera at last gets low to the ground here, though appropriately less out of any sudden stylistic shift than Ozu's shrewd attempt to film the movie from the perspective of his child protagonists. Both of the boys (all the child actors, really) are outstanding, but it's Tomio Aoki who steals it with his trademark impishness, so defiant that when he even mouths off to adults, at times he seems to intimidate even them (though his peers are always ready with a slap). The way all of the kids cry in this—bodies going stiff as a…

reviews.author: Darren Carver-Balsiger
reviews.text: A minor masterpiece, I Was Born, But... is a totally genuine and heartfelt look at childhood, youth, and innocence. It's very believable, totally inoffensive, and a perfect capturing of youth. Whilst it seems totally trivial for the first hour (but utterly captivating nonetheless), it culminates in a final act full of harsh truths and realisations, leaving it with a tinge of sadness. In particularly, it touches upon class, wealth, and social hierarchies, but maintains its childish outlook to the end, where happiness and friendship prevail even when the world is not as simple as previously thought. I Was Born, But... is utterly charming and delightful, there might not be much to it, but it's a profound and enjoyable tale.

This is a film of war games and insurrection, a satire of a world in need of revolt. If one single bullet can make a huge difference, why not change everything and gun down a school? If... is provocative, playing with conformity and rebellion as coexisting cousins. Two sides, both…

The Italian horror vibe is strong, established in the opening credits with the distinctly 70s font and washed out colours. The film is set in the early 90s, but feels older - late 70s or early 80s possibly, though it's deliberately ambiguous. Despite the Eurohorror stylings though, it's still a very British affair. In the Q&A after the film, Strickland said his biggest influence wasn't giallo but a department store called Jacksons, in his hometown of Reading. I don't know it personally but I can well imagine - I grew up frequenting these…

reviews.author: Tasha Robinson
reviews.text: Terrifically engaging film about a 16-year-old boy who starts writing about his fantasies and obsessions regarding another student and his "perfect family," and the high-school teacher who becomes voyeuristically obsessed with his stories. There's so much packed into this narrative about creators vs. fans, about art and what the audience gets out of it (as a side narrative, the teacher's wife runs a failing art gallery, and is preoccupied with finding a gimmick that will sell art to the public), and about how art can relate to reality or to wish-fulfillment. The screenplay is incredibly intelligent and dense, but the way it plays out is almost like a thriller, thanks to the direction and performances, which bring a lot of tension to what could be a low-key story about a kid writing a story. reviews.text: Out of all the books I've read, one of the most enlightening was Trickster Makes This World by Lewis Hyde. Hyde's book traces the evolution of the trickster - a boundary-crossing, rule-breaking figure from folklore and myth - from the days of tribal society through to the modern day, where its influence can be harder to see. Every time there is a controversy over explicit or offensive art, Hyde argues, we are unknowingly taking part in a re-enactment of an ancient ritual, where the trickster challenges us to confront our taboos.

Contudo, ao explorar mais a fundo a história, é possível notar que essa fluidez é obtida às custas de uma rigidez desconcentante nas expressões dos personagens, que os torna planos e sem vida. Esse aspecto é particularmente notável quando comparado ao curta-metragem anterior do diretor, Followers, que apresentava uma abordagem mais expressiva e direta. Embora possa ter sido uma escolha artística para criar uma atmosfera mais onírica, a falta de dinamismo nos personagens me distrai e impede de apreciar de forma plena o trabalho técnico empregado.

reviews.text: "Intensive Care" really comes at you like it might be a complete chore to watch, but in the actuality of things, it is absurdness that makes it all fun. George Kennedy plays Dr. Bruckner who is very clearly on the edge within his medical profession, Turned down for completing a research project and then getting into a horrific car crash, Bruckner turns into an deranged monster, attempting to slash up everything in sight. The film does have a few dry spell moments with the plot, but soon enough "Intensive Care" just embraces the fact that its completely stupid and runs with it. What works the best is that its not overly forced either, letting it be "so bad its good" through a natural feel of things. This is easily a dumb party movie, and while there are better dumb party movies out there as well, "Intensive Care" is a good beginners course kind of energy.

reviews.author: Blood Funeral Reviews
reviews.text: Intruder was a fun and entertaining little psychological slasher flick with a clown-masked killer! Intruder made up for it's lack of budget with an eerie score, some good performances, and of course, some good old fashioned blood! There are various scenes that are genuinely creepy, some which I've never seen before in microbudget horror. It also offers some nudity, which is always good in a slasher flick! The film has its fair share of solid photography choices, and some old-school video grain. It also has a fantastic sex-murder scene! One of the best I've ever seen in microbudget cinema, or just cinema in general! Very effective and neat! The movie moves at a good, fast pace. The film did what it did with straight-forwardness and wasted no time whatsoever. Intruder is a fantastic microbudget flick and I highly recommend it for fans of microbudget cinema!

reviews.text: Iphigenia is one of the most authentic-looking depictions of ancient Greece I've ever seen, and the cinematography is absolutely beautiful in every shot. The perfect score adds to the vivid atmosphere of the Trojan War era. Based on a classical tragedy from Euripides, the script is excellent. Irene Pappas as Clytemnestra and Kostas Kozakos as Agamemnon both give Oscar-worthy performances, and young Tatiana Popamoschou does an exceptional job in the title role. Director Michael Cacoyannis even manages to get a great performance out of a toddler in a non-speaking role.

reviews.author: SluggoMarx
reviews.text: Jinx Money was purportedly one of Leo Gorcey's favorite Bowery Boys films, but I found it a little underwhelming. Slip and Sach discover $50,000 in a rolled up newspaper, but a bunch of gangsters are after the dough, as is a mysterious man with an umbrella who's rubbing out the gangsters one by one. While the story is more cohesive than usual, there aren't many surprises—the identity of the man with the umbrella is telegraphed early on—and the deaths are pretty hokey. Gorcey isn't bad here and there's an excellent supporting cast that includes Sheldon Leonard and Ben Weldon as tough guys and Donald MacBride ("Jumping Butter Balls!") as a short-tempered police captain. The scenes with Leonard and MacBride are the highlights, along with a brief dream sequence in which a frightened Sach is surrounded by umbrellas.

Seriously this is a gorgeously lit movie, with spectacular sunset vistas, dancing silhouettes lit by fire light, frames lit by cigarette light. Really beautiful stuff. And while the story feels familiar, as I mentioned, it’s not necessarily predictable. I really loved Molly Parker in this. She and Moises Arias are both excellent in support roles. The themes of family and legacy are beautifully echoed with the horses as well. Horse names are often derived directly from the parents. Out of Russo’s Lamentation and Dido’s…

reviews.text: There's a fine line we tow when exposing Nazis and fascists in our outreach. In order to expose them, we often have to feature images of them - Azov Battalion with their insignias, for example - but we also keep in mind that many people barely give our media more than a glance. So, we make sure that when we show these images, it's clear to anyone only glancing at it that we are not endorsing the imagery. It's a pain in the ass, but it's important.

reviews.author: Mark Tinta
reviews.text: A largely-forgotten flop for Paramount, K2 is a big-screen expansion of the acclaimed 1982 one-act play about two climbers stranded on a ledge on Pakistan's K2, the second-highest mountain in the world. Micheal Biehn (cocky alpha lawyer) and Matt Craven (dweeby science guy devoted to his wife and kid) are mismatched best buddies who wind up on a K2 expedition bankrolled by multi-millionaire Raymond J. Barry, where asshole Biehn proceeds to pretty much piss everyone off, including old law school rival Luca Bercovici, who happens to be Barry's top climber.

reviews.author: Wesley R. Ball
reviews.text: Let's face it, there really isn't a better way to watch "Kill Bill" than this. It was originally envisioned as a massive, four hour action epic, complete with full color massacre scenes, until Tarantino declared that it was too long for mainstream audiences and decided to split it into two. To make things worse, the MPAA refused to give Kill Bill a desired R rating because of the ultra bloody scenes. To compromise, Tarantino made the offending scenes black and white, to make the blood less pronounced (I guess) and since then, the original uncut version has been all but lost.

reviews.text: taken as a whole, this is the truest "mixed bag" in tarantino's oeuvre. this just should not be one movie, seeing it all at once only magnifies how unrelated the two halves are. as an example, o-ren ishii gets like a full hour of backstory, none of the other targets get *anything*. and that makes sense when you see them as two movies, because o-ren is the final boss of part one and the villains of part two present more narratively complex obstacles. but when you see it as a single film, it just feels bizarre that we spend so much time with o-ren while bud and elle's lives are are much more subtly sketched.

reviews.author: matt lynch
reviews.text: I've got a lot wrapped up in this emotionally. It's a foundational moment in one of my very best friendships, and VOL. 1 came out just a couple months after I started working at Scarecrow, just full to bursting with references to movies I was just beginning to learn how to love. At the time, I thought I'd been waiting my whole life to see KILL BILL. Then I waited almost the same amount of time again to see this version, which is just incalculably great and the only way it should ever be watched. Even the makeshift home version you can cobble together if you have the right discs doesn't hold a candle to the real thing. While I was watching it at the Vista last night it was the best movie I have ever seen, and certainly the screening was one of the best moviegoing experiences I have ever had.

It follows a young man from a yakuza background who gets pulled into the world of kabuki theater, rising through decades of intense training, rivalries, and personal sacrifice. It’s a deep dive into the life of an onnagata (male actors who specialize in female roles), and it feels like a love letter to the art form itself.

It glosses over characters' decisions, some of which are difficult to discern. Once you get settled into a period of time it time jumps. This happens continuously. Maybe if I were more familiar with the subject and characters, it wouldn't have bothered me so much. There's also little exploration of how gender relates to Kabuki. This sets up lifelong brotherhood and pseudo rivalry, with the Hanjiro’s biological son, Shunsuke (Ryusei Yokohama), as both son and now adopted son train in the art of Kabuki. A standard is then created of unearthly and infinitely endearing romanticization. Is this incessant lyricism over-stuffed and half-baked? Maybe. If this philosophical narcissism spouted is so manufactured then why oh why does it feel so real? reviews.text: A lightweight and fun adventure targeting a younger audience, "Legends of the Hidden Temple" may be an ideal jumping-off-point for kids who will eventually devour "Raiders of the Lost Ark" and "The Mummy." While those two adventure greats and their ilk may bear too much bite for the elementary school crowd, Joe Menendez' trek through the dangers and mythology at play in an ancient jungle temple offers an ideal blend of wit, thrills, and menace for that age group. Spry and quick-paced, the film looks good for its Nickelodeon pedigree, boasts an engaging energy, and features an investable quest and cast of characters. Even grownups will get a kick out of the hidden temple and its associated legends.

reviews.text: Por momentos da la impresión de que las barreras que Martel pone -el límite hasta donde le permite acercarse- impiden que el documental llegue a las profundidades que naturalmente podría haber alcanzado. Abramovich toma la inteligente decisión de incorporar esos límites al punto de convertirlos en el tema del documental. Entiende, o postula, a la dirección como un proceso de delimitación. Dirigir sería marcar los bordes de algo para que su forma ideal aparezca, y usa a Martel en plena acción para graficarlo.Es algo muy interesante si tenemos en cuenta que en la poética de Abramovich los límites son importantísimos. ¿Qué se ve y qué no? parece ser una pregunta crucial a la hora de entender su concepción de la puesta en escena, y en ese sentido Años Luz es (como no podía ser de otra manera) más una declaración de principios de Abramovich que una puerta de entrada para entender la idea de cine de Martel.

reviews.author: Jerry
reviews.text: After a sublimely ballsy opening, this flick hits all of the nihilistic beats one expects from your standard poliziotteschi fare. Sociopathic cops, jarring English musical cues, amorality on- and offscreen, a sheen of grime—unfortunately, its pacing is about as clunky as its title, although just as ludicrously badass. There is enough to keep you entertained and intrigued, plus, the dynamic between the two leads is a pleasant intermingling of hardly veiled homoeroticism and humorous insanity. But it sure does take its time getting where it’s going, and it’s a bit too cartoonish for my blood. Could’ve cut it down to like 88 minutes and it probably would have benefited greatly. Passable spaghetti sleaze, but I have seen better.

reviews.text: I do not know if the name of Laurent Micheli's film Lola is a reference to the popular Kinks song about a trans woman. What is obvious, however, is the power of real-life trans actress Mya Bollaers' debut performance as the titular heroine. Everything about the character of Lola exudes realism. The adversity in her life is similar to what countless trans folks have experienced in a world that discriminates against us at every turn with both micro and macro-aggressions. Instead of having surgery like she had anticipated, Lola loses her mother unexpectedly and must go on a road trip with her angry, bigoted father, Philippe (Benoit Magimel).

reviews.text: Inspired, ingenious, pure and sincere, there're very few films out there like this and it's really a shame. Tsui Hark strings us along for what seems like a typical rom-com slapstick at the beginning before abruptly expelling us into several other dimensions of cinema at the drop of a hat, and the rest of the film becomes an exercise in execution, almost more a showing of a magician's bag of tricks rather than a film outlined by a tight narrative, but given the tricks at play I don't think many would complain. In doing so it builds upon itself, never losing sight of its rom-com origins but layering over it with inventive techniques that push the two lovers-to-be closer together…

reviews.author: Sean Gilman
reviews.text: Oh just your typical mashup of Back to the Future, Ghost, Cantonese Opera, Looney Tunes and vomit jokes. The least well-known of Tsui Hark's four films from 1995 but it might be the best. The Blade is a dark as hell ultra-violent wuxia film, The Chinese Feast a farce about food and community, and this one an effects-driven, period romantic comedy. (I haven't seen the fourth, The Lovers, which like this one also stars Charlie Yeung and Nicky Wu, yet). What a year.

reviews.author: SupremeLemon (지존레몬)
reviews.text: A staggering confluence of visual and sonic experimentation in a meta-cinematic universe, one that calls for an immanent conception of corporeal and incorporeal existence. Body and spirit are broken down and reconstituted before our eyes, deeply and eagerly attuned to the potentialities and manifold meanings of human connection. All of this is contained within a narrative framework where spatiotemporal boundaries and aesthetic dimensions routinely collide and ultimately coalesce with each other. The result is an exuberant kind of syncretic theatricality that celebrates love in all its myriad forms. My kind of Asian Baby Girl/Fuccboi cinema 🥰

reviews.author: fivepoisonskid
reviews.text: tsui hark's strange experimentation with cgi might have come to its fruition in this magical film. while american cgi is typically praised it reaches some semblance of verisimilitude (e.g. jurassic park), tsui's cgi revels in artificiality in order to create striking fantastical images. in this respect one could compare tsui's approach to, say, the matte paintings in hitchcock's marnie, but that would be somewhat inaccurate because cgi for tsui, certainly in this film, is a matter of elevating emotion rather than hitchcock's distanciation. in other words, tsui hark is firmly self-aware of cgi's inherent spectacle and seems to embrace it with sincerity whether for humorous purposes (kong's facial contortions and hovering punctuation) or the stuff of nightmares (the lampost purgatory littered with hazy obelisks and scattered anatomy).

reviews.text: Throughout his daring and unforgettable career, Spanish director José Ramón Larraz created some of the most essential and powerful works of the seventies and eighties. Las alumnas de madame Olga (1981) is not one of them. In fact, this is far and away the worst Larraz film I have seen and the only one that I found, dare I say, boring. I saw one commenter here mention that it doesn't seem like Larraz's heart is in this one and, yeah, totally. MADAME OLGA'S PUPILS is also an example of a great director slumming and there's just very little to recommend. Larraz is a great enough director as to where he isn't going to deliver anything less than competent and that's…

reviews.text: With the upcoming release of Alberto Sedano's documentary on Spanish 'Clasificada 'S'' films, I've been watching a few of the films to get a better sense of them beyond the ones I'd already seen (Franco, Naschy, but mostly Franco). At their best, these movies can be inventive and transgressive both in terms of their subject matter (Naschy's 'El Caminante') and style (Franco's 'Night Has a Thousand Desires'). Or they can be just plain wild, brimming with manic exuberance ('Satan's Blood', 'Black Candles').

reviews.text: Im Original eine offensichtlich zahnlose und von ihren schwierigen Produktionsbedingungen gezeichnete Horrorkomödie, die in der deutschen Synchronisation allerdings zur absoluten Höchstform aufläuft. Dafür nahm das Team rund um Michael Richter ("Das Söldnerkommando") umfangreiche Kürzungen vor, um das Tempo zu beschleunigen, ersetzte die Musik von Riz Ortolani teilweise durch Tiny Tims "Tiptoe Through the Tulips" und legte allen Akteuren abstruseste Wortspiele in den Mund (selbst wenn sie der Kamera gerade den Rücken zudrehen) oder lässt sie der Einfachheit halber nur unverständliches Kauderwelsch brabbeln (Arnold Marquis in seiner wohl anspruchslosesten Sprechrolle als Butler!). Kein Wunder, dass bei den Freiheiten, die man sich in der Synchronisation genommen hat, auch im eingedeutschten Vorspann anstatt von "Drehbuch" lieber gleich von "Lyrik und Prosa" schreibt. Für diejenigen, die keine wortgetreue Übersetzung benötigen, ein Heidenspaß.

reviews.author: Revue
reviews.text: Visually, it's pretty damn strong, with energetic and cartoony animation and some nice designs, colours and art direction. Unfortunately, while it has its moments, it particularly loses itself in the last 1/5 or so; while it isn't convoluted like I've seen claimed, it is bland. The logic makes sense, up and until the end, where the solution to the fairly interesting issue of selfish wishes is quite contrived, unproportionate, and cloying. I also find the main guy character a bit irritating and tropey, and the same goes for the grandmother. This could've been a great film had it taken a more interesting approach to handling it's main conundrum, and/or had it embraced fun cartooniness above rote spectacle and an overly dramatic anime melodrama climax. Someone needs to give Hirao a way better script and let him do more ridiculous camera angles and layouts etc., that's where he excels - basically I want more of Manabi Straight's OP lol.

reviews.author: Movie Good or Movie Bad?
reviews.text: Learned of this oddity a few days ago with news of Meet the Parents 4, and it’s deeply sad to know Universal has done so much to bury a film they bought the rights for in order to have made the much more famous Ben Stiller and Robert De Niro starring Meet the Parents. There is a similar framework and gags here, but as where in the version of the film people are more familiar with the humor comes from the ribbing of Stiller’s character and how comically mean De Niro is, there is intentional framing of everything through a lens of cringe, awkward, and dark humor. Lots of these gags don’t have room to breathe, we simply shift from scenario to scenario, before the film plunges into darkness and while I didn’t enjoy this more than the other version of the film, there is a discomfort here that is delightful.

Being the only thing he knows how to do well, he accepts a job somewhere in Southeast Asia with the rest of his team where his target happens to be a mixture of local bandits but also good hearted civilians. This becomes divisive, leading to Lundgren's character of Nick and a grouping of his team that have some moral fiber to make a stand with the civilian people against a grouping of the bad mercs who join up with some of the local low life…

reviews.text: Co-written by "Lone Star" filmmaker John Sayles, "Men of War" is a surprisingly soulful drama exploring colonialism and exploitation...that also doubles as a kick-ass mercenary action flick?! I have to thank my man Daniel Gorman for inspiring me to finally watch this one. It's long been one of my Dolph Lundgren blindspots; now not only do I know why Dolph's character is named Gunner in "The Expendables" movies, but I'd likely argue this is a superior men-on-a-mission action flick than any of the "Expendables" movies themselves.

reviews.text: Another severely underrated entry in the book of Dolph, this men on a mission movie sans Predator (but with a very similar score) has enough style and surprises to hold its own if you ask me. A rock solid cast with B.D. Wong, Tiny Lister, Charlotte Lewis, Catherine Bell as a bit of a Lady Rambo, and Trevor Goddard aka KANO from Mortal Kombat, choking on the beautiful island scenery. I'm being a bit generous with my rating, but it's to offset its current average which is unjustly low. If you like this type of movie, and don't mind a bit of dumbass macho bullshit, you likely won't get bored by this. A solid ass summer pick where a lot of people get blown up 💥👍

reviews.author: AndrewC
reviews.text: As with stuff like Joshua Tree and Silent Trigger, Men of War is a pretty solid 90s Dolph Lundgren action vehicle that might be DTV-level and obviously not expensive, but is still a good deal of fun. For this, it works nicely as a straightforward men-on-a-mission action pic that has Dolph leading a fairly decent cast with a handful of recognizable faces in a story that's conventional, but works as the kind of movie it is. From there, Men of War assembles some solid action sequences (the final half-hour is basically one long battle) and gets it all done in an entertaining fashion typical of its lead's better efforts from this time.

Anyone calling this "boring" probably just wanted to watch Dolph Lundgren incinerate people with a grenade launcher without all the melancholy self-reflection. Fortunately I love both.

reviews.author: Blake Bergman "Various Spaghetti"
reviews.text: "Michael Collins" is a 1996 drama directed by Neil Jordan. As the title of the film directly suggests, the film is about Michael Collins who was a prominent figure in the fight for Irish independence dating back to the 1910s. The film revolves around him and his affiliated soldiers in the fight as most of their warfare was waged in the shadows or in secret, due to the sheer overwhelming size of their British opposition. The real Michael Collins himself lived from 1890 to 1922, and the film makes good on his portrayal, placing Liam Neeson in the central role.

reviews.text: The most conventional aspect of Missing is that Ed and Beth are on opposite sides of the political spectrum, and a number of their scenes together are him trying to reckon with her “kooky leftist views” that spit in the face of his conservative Christian Science. That Missing is helmed by one star from Old Hollywood (Lemmon) and one star from New Hollywood (Spacek) lends it an interesting air of legitimacy, so to speak. It’s not only that the horrible events of the film are happening, but they are happening to beloved Americans! The indignity! The injustice! The film goes so far to say as much just that near its conclusion, in which one of the sniveling U.S. diplomats says something to the effect that Lemmon’s Ed would not even care what the United States is doing in another country were he not personally involved.

My main complaint is that Clarke Peters didn't get more time and presence, but when you have Bob Hoskins taking center stage, I will forgive even such an egregious error. It's not a feminist gangster noir, but it's still got empathy for queer sex workers--if this were a cop story, they'd be expendable dumpster-filler. Here, they're at least people. Hoskins treats everyone with his gruff compassion, so the patronization feels a little less patronizing and the embarrassing love story feels like a critique of men's fantasies. Hoskins takes the role and makes it human in a way that emphasizes that despite the occasional cliche, this is a personal story,…

reviews.text: The characters in this film act unpredictably and that is doubly true for Bob Hoskins’s George. Towards the end of the film George shoots any and all growth he’s made in the foot, unveiling the sadness laying beneath his actions. And while it’s frustrating to watch, and near impossible to support, it’s easy to understand. There’s something so utterly human about needing to be wanted and wanting to be needed, and the way we collapse into ourselves when we realize we are neither. At least not anymore. At times a romp, other times genuinely unnerving and incredibly dark, this was a fantastic surprise.

reviews.text: I really hope Pavel Talankin will be okay. He took a huge risk making a film that Vladimir Putin would consider treasonous. I can't believe the risks he took. Pavel is a teacher filled with positivity, warmth and a kind of endearing dorky sense of humor. He's an individual in a place where conformity is the norm. We watch as his happy-go-lucky spirit is stripped away. Once the invasion of Ukraine began schools were mandated to follow a strict script of propaganda. Since Pavel is the school's videographer he's able to capture the drastic change. We watch as the kids' innocence and happiness drain away.

reviews.text: Mr. Vampire is an action/comedy/horror hybrid that succeeds on all three counts and may be the best "hopping vampire" film of them all. reviews.text: A pretty stupid and often boring TV movie with the title event being only one of way too many pointless plots. And they don't even handle the murder part well. It's about a man who was rejected by the Houston Astros taking revenge with a plot to kidnap a player's wife and hold her for ransom. But from the very beginning he messes up and takes the wrong woman. From there it's one fuck up after another and it strains credibility mightily. So many easily preventable things go wrong, many from sheer carelessness and poor planning. It was my thought that doing something like this is more likely to make you hyper-aware, making the plotting here absurd. And whenever it's not focused on this fuck-up, the screenplay spends time with various dull, thinly-written characters who you couldn't care less about. A pretty decent cast is completely wasted on this tripe.

Glad I didn’t see this as a teen at time of release - probably would have wrong-headedly found it a dull middle-brow “chick flick”. The inimitable Sally Field (director Martin Ritt’s Norma Rae star of Oscar glory) works an Alice Doesn’t Live Here Anymore vibe playing a cash strapped single Mom trying to jump start her life on a dilapidated ranch in small town Arizona. reviews.author: chavel
reviews.text: A moseying romance, with outmoded troubles and maybe outmoded in a lot of other areas, too. Murphy’s Romance makes Sally Field a hard-luck single mother attempting to redo her life on the horse ranches of a very shaggy Arizona town and James Garner as the older and wiser pharmacist who helps out this very distressed momma. Field is supposed to be plucky, but is just gosh plain here. The reason why this very poky romantic drama is watchable at all, and made me look up at it, is because of Garner’s inimitable gentlemanliness. He has a way of purring through his lines in a way that made me envious. I like his style with his cowboy vests, too. Makes for some nice and harmless background noise.

reviews.author: Sally Jane Black
reviews.text: Somehow far more chaotic than its pace suggests, this film feels like it should be calmer and simpler, observational. Instead, the film's animation style and sense of humor infuse it with energy even in its quieter moments. Underlying many of the vignettes are commentaries on masculinity and the shifts in family/gender roles culturally, but the film doesn't seem to either endorse nor denounce. Rather, it observes and honors the strength of its women characters, showing not only that the perceived shifts are less shifts in actual power and more shifts in understandings of what has often been. The film isn't perfect in this regard; a deeper analysis would probably yield mixed results. But overall, the mixture of whimsy and thoughtfulness, of pace and tone, makes up for any minor issues.

reviews.text: January has been unexpectedly stacked for horror fans, and Ryan Prows’ grittily humorous, socially charged vampire-thriller, Night Patrol, kept the ball rolling wonderfully. Through a cast that I can only assume will age like a fine wine over time, Night Patrol offers a sleazy fun, exploitative slice of stylish horror, which both warrants a relaxation of one’s critical film brain, while also offering critiques on societal and police structuring without beating its viewer over the head. At the end of the day, we get a fairly likable set of Bloods and Crips putting aside lifelong vendettas while believing in shapeshifters, energy pyramids, Zulu warriors and vamp-demons to battle a gang of undead police officers. Very fun genre stuff.

reviews.author: Rosie✨
reviews.text: Nightmare Cinema is a horror anthology that brings together five strangers trapped in a cursed theater. Each is forced to face their deepest fears through a series of frightening films that blur the line between reality and nightmare. Mickey Rourke plays the projectionist, but his character feels completely interchangeable—anyone could have filled the role. The anthology features five short stories, none of which are particularly memorable. I won’t dive too deep into each one, but they all feel a bit uneven in execution. The acting, aside from Elizabeth Reaser’s solid performance, tends to be stiff. Many of the actors seem to be reading their lines directly from a script rather than having a natural conversation. The gore effects are impressive when done practically, though the CGI is often jarring and subpar. Despite these issues, the stories themselves remain interesting enough. Overall, I didn’t hate it.

Parts of this are quite effectively eerie and Ole Bornedal clearly is a skilled director, but it's not a very coherently-told story and there's some wild tonal clashes in the first two acts that don't mesh. Thankfully, the third act is a major improvement and the cast is stacked with so many great actors that Nightwatch mostly succeeds at being a solid serial killer horror thriller that's got some pretty good things to it.

reviews.text: An anthology, or rather a nightmare of nightmares. A film put to bed with death by domesticity, deriving tension from the claustrophobic stillness of bathrooms, bedrooms and kitchens thoroughly lived in yet unsettled by the uncanny. Lift the towels from the wash basket and watch the room be enveloped in many a shade of gelled fluorescence, or pull open the shoji and witness the malformed goblin scurrying upon the trail of a human scent. This is bookended by fairy tales and sustained by Yumi's successive demise(s), adopting storytelling as a matter of prompts - a birthday wish, a photo book, a start screen, a fantastical recitation - that call forth the human condition of emotional horror. From accidents come anger,…

reviews.author: Stephen M
reviews.text: This must be my week to watch suburban angst films. After watching 1997’s The Ice Storm a few days ago, I checked out the 1950s version, Martin Ritt’s No Down Payment. Although there’s an element of soap opera in this tale of four couples in one of the many “developments” that sprung up in the postwar years, it carries a strong social critique of the underside of the white middle-class suburban lifestyle, funded by loans from the GI Bill. The pressure to conform, consume and succeed, underlying class issues, alcoholism, infidelity, racism, marital conflict and rape: they’re all there in the pleasant little California subdivision of Sunrise Hills.

reviews.text: During a meteor shower, an alien creature lands in the small California town of Liberty. The creature feeds on electricity, so it sure is fortuitous that Liberty is the site of a brand new power plant going online that very weekend. Formula filmmaking by director Jon Hess (ALLIGATOR II) finds the alien knocking off townspeople in gruesome ways — nothing too graphic or gory, but enough to keep the effects guys busy all through production. The practical monster effects are pretty good, but the decision to slather them with animated electricity was the wrong one.

reviews.text: This is a stale bag of pretzels. Every character is safely vanilla in almost every way, like they just stepped off the set of a Hallmark sitcom. The main lady looks like she's always dressed for a church function; the sheriff tucks his shirt into his jeans like a psychopath; the most villainous thing the movie’s antagonist does is tell dad jokes; and the town doctor is just a younger Wilford Brimley with a sheared mustache stain and superior cardio. The only character with any sort of personality sizzle is the random search party dude who has strands of sticky saliva stuck to his lips and you start to wonder why he wouldn’t wipe that shit with a napkin before mingling with other people. But everybody else is off-brand oatmeal shavings and you won’t care what happens to any of them.

reviews.author: Criterion
reviews.text: Tsui Hark returned to the director’s chair for the rollicking comedic adventure Once Upon a Time in China V, in which the indomitable hero Wong Fei-hung (Vincent Zhao) tangles with a band of ruthless, finger-removing pirates who are exploiting the political chaos created by the invasion of foreigners in order to terrorize the Chinese coast. The fist-and-foot kung-fu set pieces—including a showstopping, gold-hued melee set in a warehouse of pirate treasure—are plentiful, but Tsui ups the ante by introducing acrobatic gunplay to the proceedings, infusing this furiously entertaining crowd-pleaser with a bracing jolt of John Woo–style bullet ballet mayhem.

reviews.author: More_Badass
reviews.text: These non-Jet Li entires are pretty overlooked, but Once Upon A Time In China V turned out to be my favorite since the original. When the opening ends with a pirate gun-spear slicing off hands, there’s no doubt that Tsui Hark is back in the director’s seat. Rosamund Kwan and Xiong Xin-Xin’s Club Foot return as well. Vincent Zhao is still a blander Wong Fei-Hung, but he comes into his own thanks to a story that’s much more unique compared to 3 and 4.

reviews.author: Sean Gilman
reviews.text: Tsui Hark is back as director, and Rosamund Kwan returns, but Jet Li is still missing. The story picks up where the last one left off, with Wong Fei-hung and his family and friends heading south after the failure of the Boxer Rebellion. They meet up with Aunt 13 and Porky Lam (back for the first time since the first film) and get waylaid by pirates before they can flee to Hong Kong.

reviews.text: One More Shot takes another swig at the well-worn time loop formula, this time with a ‘90s nostalgia chaser and a splash of quarter-life crisis. Emily Browning stars as Minnie, a woman stuck reliving New Year’s Eve 1999 every time she downs a shot of her mysteriously time-warping tequila. With each trip back to Y2K Eve, she attempts to course-correct her life, rekindle an old flame, and maybe—just maybe—land on a future worth taking into the next millennium.It’s not Groundhog Day or Palm Springs, but it’s got its own buzz. Browning’s effortless charm goes a long way. I would have loved more 90’s nostalgia, obviously. The time loop shenanigans are mostly predictable, but the film is breezy and self-aware enough to keep things entertaining.[Best of SXSW 2025: Comedies]

reviews.author: K Gray
reviews.text: The best documentaries are the ones like this without overbearing narration or overwhelming facts but rather an immersive space of real life events and moving experiences that speak for themself. This politically charged doc uses home footage, recorded phone calls, news archives, interviews, concerts, and commercials to create a powerful expression of what the early 70s American revolution looked and felt like with John Lennon, Yoko Ono, and friends at the forefront. It’s less about the controversy or romance of their relationship and instead an intense focus on their passionate union to impart peace, justice, and freedom to a country in need. It’s a powerful portrait that demonstrates the kind of identity and values Lennon longed for after his departure…

reviews.text: I’m a bit taken aback by how effortlessly this manages to maintain its sense of humor and mounting stakes despite how often the jokes completely derail the narrative. There’s a real stop-go-stop-go rhythm to this that normally should not work and yet Over Your Dead Body thrives because of it. Downside is there’s a lengthy bit associated with sexual assault that goes on for way too long and sucks most of the oxygen out of the room as it drags on. My theater was virtually completely sold out and the crowd was eating this movie up until that scene. Whole vibe shifted in a really noticeable way. Luckily, the film manages to mostly recover after it, but it does leave a lingering aftertaste that does sour the whole thing. Still fun, still quite funny, just… a little less than ideal.

reviews.author: Christopher Fujino
reviews.text: This was supposedly made because Miyazaki & Takahata couldn't secure the rights to Pippi Longstocking, and it's an obvious precursor to My Neighbor Totoro (right down to the title song). But the children's story I was reminded of while watching Panda! Go Panda! was The Many Adventures of Winnie the Pooh, with it's serial/anthology of shorts format, and premise of idyllic childhood autonomy in a non-threatening world. But the strength of Winnie the Pooh is how funny the characterizations of the animals are (Eeyore is depressed, Rabbit is a neurotic compulsive, Owl a know-it-all who knows nothing, et al), and characterization is sorely lacking here, especially from the supporting characters.

reviews.text: "Panic Attack!" or "Ataque de pánico!" is a 2009 Uruguayan short film created by Fede Álvarez. It's a brief unique use of CGI to capture the feel of some old school atomic age robots and other alien forces attacking a city. While today it's something that we sequentially see a dime for a dozen, at the time the video became a real conductive piece of craftmanship that drew the attention of Ghost House Pictures, giving director Alvarez the eventual segway into creating "Evil Dead" (2013). It's a unique brief watch that is worth viewing for the time it was created and the gateway it became for its director.

reviews.text: Feeling pretty blown away by this. Satoshi Kon’s work is some of the most terrifying to me because of how he effortlessly creates a space in your head. ‘Internal’ is probably the best word to describe it and while that may seem intriguing, any of his films would suggest the opposite. With ‘Perfect Blue’ and ‘Paprika’ he accomplishes so much with so little, taking high-concept ideas and boiling them down to their most electrifying parts. That said, you can imagine what a +300 minute Kon mini-series could do.

reviews.text: Satoshi Kon was truly one of a kind. His presence is still sorely missed today. As my taste in film has shifted over the years — not always for the better — Kon has remained one of the most tantalizing and singular voices in all of cinema, in my opinion. As an impressionable dumb kid, watching Perfect Blue for the first time blew my peanut-sized brain into a thousand pieces. Not only did it open my eyes to this entirely different approach to storytelling, but introduced me to the wonderfully creative world of Anime — a genre I had all but written off at that point.

reviews.text: Passage to Marseille was pretty good, showcasing the expert direction of the great Michael Curtiz. While it definitely doesn’t reach the heights of Casablanca, it still delivers an engaging wartime drama with strong performances, particularly from Humphrey Bogart—who once again proves he’s Hollywood’s greatest Frenchman, despite sounding about as Parisian as a New York City cab driver. The film’s non-linear storytelling keeps things interesting, and there are several exciting and suspenseful moments that stand out. The cinematography and atmosphere effectively capture the tension and stakes of the story. While it may not be Curtiz’s best, it’s a solid and well-crafted film that I enjoyed. I’d definitely recommend it, especially to fans of classic war films.

Also contains more Peter Lorre than Casablanca, which counts for a lot.

reviews.text: Warner Bros spent a lot of resources during the mid-1940s trying to recreate the success of Casablanca. This film is one of the most obvious examples. It re-teams producer Hal Wallis, director Michael Curtiz, composer Max Steiner (whose score again uses “La Marseilles” prominently), editor Owen Marks, and several of the actors from Casablanca (Humphrey Bogart, Claude Rains, Peter Lorre, Sydney Greenstreet, Helmut Dantine, and Corinna Mura). But it lacks Casablanca’s compelling story and deeply felt subtexts. In fact, it’s a good example of a film that has most of the elements it needs to be a classic — except a strong screenplay. reviews.text: Martin Ritt’s sensitive, matter of fact approach to directing produced any number of sweet, touching films, chief among them HUD and NORMA RAE. He lets actors have their space, allowing small moments time to land, and this lends his films a sense of authenticity. There’s no flashy camera work and he never had a preferred genre, having crafted Westerns, spy thrillers, romances, and social problem films. But movies like SOUNDER and THE SPY WHO CAME IN FROM THE COLD are as good as they get.

reviews.text: Piercing is captivating retro-style horror that's quirky, slick, and bloody. Christopher Abbot plays Reed, a man leaving his loving wife and newborn to go on a business trip, however, it's not a normal business trip. He's sinisterly plotting a murder of an escort. This takes a complicated turn when the original escort he hired couldn't make it and it doesn't go as planned when a different girl, played by Mia Wasikowska, shows up. Stellar performances from Abbot and Wasikowska. Set pieces and designs with bold colors were fantastic, it builds up the unsettling feeling of being in an enclosed space. The soundtrack, tone, and pacing were great too. I was with this until the ending, which was not as strong. The rest of the film was a sharp dark satire.

Polanski and co. so desperately want you to have fun but it's obvious they don't believe a second of it—Polanski is incapable. It's entirely in Gaelic, which is novel, especially since it's such an endangered language now. But its vibrancy, and urgency, and grittiness are its greatest strengths, surprising coming out of a culture that had no film industry to speak of before this. reviews.text: Five years before "Scream" was born the lesser-known "Popcorn" partially anticipated what Wes Craven perfected with his meta horror milestone and would establish it as a brilliant innovation within the genre that was copied countless times from that point. Herrier also tries to take up the concept of shamelessly exaggerated self-referentiality by making not a horror movie in the classic sense, but a movie about the fascination of horror movies and the special value of the spectacle that they often bring up. The flick is from the early nineties, but it feels rooted in the eighties and creates the according mood and atmosphere. "Popcorn" is wonderfully imaginative, but overall the entertainment value is rather mediocre.

The always great Jill Schoelen stars as one of the students who has been having weird nightmares surrounding some kind of cinema cult and naturally its not long before her fellow students start being picked off. reviews.author: Justin Decloux
reviews.text: I always wish we had gotten more 100% pure Godfrey Ho films. PRINCESS MADAM is as deranged as the inserts he provided for his infamous ninja films, but the novelty with MADAM is that it's a constant flow of entertainment. Godfrey jumps from top-shelf Girls with Guns action to downbeat John Woo inspired Heroic Bloodshed with an impressive dedication to delivering the goods. It's surprisingly progressive for the sub-genre (which often stranded the women heroes as supporting characters) simply by keeping the two partners front and center - while all the men are portrayed as adulterers, wimps, or traitorous bad guys. No lies detected.

reviews.text: Aqua was a test of Flow's concept, but this short feels way closer to the style and overall atmosphere of that film. The animation may be rough, but it was made by a very young and less experienced animator with no real budget. The 3D models may look very simplistic, but the shot compositions, music, and overall sound design does give it a cinematic feel to it. Or at the very least, it looks like an immersive VR game. Gints Zilbalodis is an animator, composer, editor, sound designer and gamer! The man is absolutely talented! Not only did he earn that Oscar, but there's a mural of the black cat from Flow on the side of a building in the capital of Poland! That's amazing!

reviews.text: Priorities is a touchingly delicate animated short from Gints Zilbalodis which sees him chiefly experimenting with long takes. It follows a man stranded on an isolated island with his dog, becoming confronted increasingly with the canine wanting to play and be acknowledged; however, the man merely wants to escape and leave the island behind. It emphasises the requirements of being aware and taking satisfaction in the more immediate things in life even though they may seem contradictory to more immediate requisites. I'm very much a dog person, so I found this short to be rather delightful.

reviews.text: "Rest in Pieces" is a 1987 supernatural slasher film directed by Jose Ramon Larraz. Larraz was known at times for using an alternate name under his credited listing, to which this film uses "Joseph Braunstein" in place of his name. As stated earlier, the film is an interesting blend of supernatural flavorings as well as that of the slasher horror brand. In this manner of things, the film executes in a far cleverer application than what I expected, even though it absolutely holds that kitschy "straight-to-video" energy about it.

reviews.text: ‎Cinema continues to amaze me. Just when I think I’ve seen everything a film has to offer, a film like this comes along and surprises me with its boldness, its innovation, and the shocks it delivers through purely cinematic means. This film contains many things I’ve never encountered before: images and techniques that feel entirely new, as if someone is stretching cinema’s skin from the inside. Watching it was an experience unlike any other, much like the journey of one hundred years of film history through various films and styles. Each chapter of the film has a different body, a different mood, and a different rhythm than the previous one. Like a rollercoaster, the film keeps moving forward through every…

reviews.author: Matt Neglia
reviews.text: RESURRECTION is an awe-inspiring ode to cinematic language that reaffirms Bi Gan’s status as one of the most masterful filmmakers working today. A mesmerizing, out-of-body experience, it features stunning visuals across six chapters, each evoking one of the five human senses. Often confounding but always captivating, whether through its use of expressionism, film noir, a heartwarming father-daughter story, another glorious, technically dazzling oner, or a transcendent final shot that simply took my breath away (Did I happen to mention there’s vampires too?), few films are operating on this level of visionary artistry. It’s the kind of work that inspires a generation to pick up a camera & put their dreams up on the silver screen.

reviews.text: Unlike anything else you’ll see made today. Fragmented dream-like storytelling, reviving old cinematic styles and urging us to dream. Shapeshifting through eras, with the constant mirrored reflections changing reality. And man, the staging in this thing? Genius - I couldn't take my eyes off it. Can’t remember the last time I watched something so absurdly creative from start to finish, with each inch of space used as a weapon to completely break my mind. From the deep greys to the neon-soaked frames: it's hypnotising. Each chapter offers such a new feel, connecting through the film's formal evolutions. It’s chaos, yet such a statement piece. No idea what just happened. Catnip for fellas like me.

reviews.author: Thomas Flight
reviews.text: Cinema as metamodern mythology. A swirling synthesis of film history expressed through style. Bi Gan’s Resurrection takes us through a series of dreams, dreamt by a monster whose insides plays reels of film. It opens with an expressionistic silent film, evocative of early German works, and proceeds to shape shift for each new dream, becoming a film noir, melodrama, and culminating in an impressive single-take sequence that traverses streetlight and rain-drenched alleyways on New Years Eve 1999.

reviews.text: I’m usually not a fan of the heartwarming “overcoming tragedy” genre, but I watched this for Mélanie Laurent and Pio Marmaï. Although beautifully shot and well acted, my heart remained unwarmed for the first half or so. But then I gradually began to fall under the movie’s spell, largely thanks not to the adult leads but to young actor Carmen Kassovitz. The climactic race strained credibility a bit (could they really have gotten away with that with all those cameras around?), but I didn’t really care since by that point I was fighting back tears. Laurent’s final line—“deux femmes”—also got me right in the feels.

reviews.author: Jonathan White
reviews.text: Finally, after 44 years, I’ve watched Ryan’s Daughter. This is rather significant, as David Lean is one of my favourite directors, and his ‘epic’ period produced some of my all time favourite films. Bridge on the River Kwai, Lawrence of Arabia, and my long time favourite Doctor Zhivago. For years I’ve been afraid to watch Ryan’s Daughter because of vague remembrances of critical reviews. I really didn’t want to watch a ‘bad’ Lean epic and risk tarnishing my love and respect for the aforementioned masterpieces. Each one of them has touched me in a particular way with their characters, visuals, and score. No one seems to mention Ryan’s Daughter. How can it possibly stand up to the experiences I’ve been…

It is very methodical, awful paced, but it replaces the imposed romantic sweep of his 60s movies for some actual madness even more so because how the intimate human drama plays against those huge scope vistas. I appreciate how much Lean take his time and the large texture he achieves on the village and there's some very satisfying in how it allows Mitchum/Miles scenes playing against the more lustful relationship she has with Jones. As a spin on Madame Bovary, it carries more ideas than most. As a career summation it marries early and late Lean in a way none of his other work do even if some might…

reviews.author: legolas
reviews.text: I get why Ryan’s Daughter faced the backlash it did when it was first released. It’s a film that arrived with so much expectation trailing behind it, expectations that ended up shaping, maybe even distorting, how people saw it. Audiences and critics were anticipating another David Lean epic on the scale of Lawrence of Arabia or Doctor Zhivago, with something grand, sprawling, operatic. What they got instead was something more internal, more emotionally subdued. And for many, that dissonance between what they expected and what Lean actually delivered was too jarring to reconcile.

reviews.text: As someone who has enjoyed every “Scream” film, SCREAM 7 was the first one to truly let me down from beginning (Justice for Melissa Barrera and #FreePalestine) to absurd, hollow end. The once clever tropes are now worn out, and while the brutal kills are staged well, they mean very little when they’re inflicted on characters we’re given little reason to care about. The messy story leans too heavily on nostalgia and the ultimate reveal is completely ridiculous and underwhelming. There’s also a missed opportunity to have any sort of meaningful commentary on the use of deepfakes and AI technology. To her credit, Neve Campbell delivers one of her best performances in the series and Isabel May certainly holds her own, but seven films in, I think it’s about time we let Sidney Prescott rest in peace and this once beloved franchise burn.

reviews.author: Lou (rhymes with wow!)
reviews.text: Septet is a seven-part anthology movie with segments directed by some of the biggest names in Hong Kong's cinematic new wave movement. The segments are actually more about a variety of people in Hong Kong through out the decades than that they are about the city itself, but perhaps that's semantics? Most of them rely heavily on nostalgia and some are autobiographical.

reviews.author: Filipe Furtado
reviews.text: Less a movie about Hong Kong than a last hurrah for Hong Kong cinema as defined by the new wave generation. Very nostalgic although the point of view is very much a discourse from the present. This is the rare omnibus that feel actually thought out in a manner that makes the qualities of individual episodes less important than the overall image they generate. It does end with a Tsui directed nonsense that after 90 minutes about the city through its last 7 decades curtain call everything in a studio set mental institution with comedy predicted in disappearing into itself.

reviews.author: Cody Franklin
reviews.text: Very enjoyable documentary told from recordings by Serling. It takes a bit to get started and the reenactments are off putting, but once it gets going, it rolls. I've always been interested in the early days a television and the intellects/talent involved with the development. To see how they deal with a medium that eventually dumbs down and pushes them out should be a mini series. Serling was an fascinating and talented individual who was always on the right side of history and had a firm belief that his audience wasn't morons. His recordings and interviews are direct, passionate, and still reflect today. I could listen to this man talk for hours.

reviews.author: Hammertonail
reviews.text: Born in 1924, the great Rod Serling, creator of The Twilight Zone—one of the best television series of all time—lived through tumultuous times and emerged with a deep commitment to social justice and speaking his mind. Though he died of a heart attack at the far-too-young age of 50, in 1975, he left behind an artistic legacy to make anyone proud. In Serling, director Jonah Tulis’ thoroughly engaging new documentary about the man, we get all the cinematic and real-life goods a fan could desire, with a plethora of detail to satisfy newcomers to the topic, as well.

reviews.author: Andre 1904
reviews.text: John Frankenheimer's smart, tense Cold War political thriller about a high-ranking U.S. Marine Colonel (Kirk Douglas) who discovers that a popular four-star general (Burt Lancaster) is plotting a military coup to overthrow the President (Fredric March). What follows is a gripping game of cat-and-mouse set inside the corridors of power in Washington. Frankenheimer’s direction is crisp and efficient, and the script crackles with sharp, intelligent dialogue. Both Lancaster and Douglas are excellent, Lancaster radiates charismatic authority, while Douglas carries the moral weight of the story. The film’s exploration of loyalty, democracy, and the dangers of unchecked military power still feels disturbingly relevant.While the suspense is strong, the romantic subplot feels a little dated and the middle section is occasionally talk-heavy. Still, it’s a solid, well-acted political drama that holds up nicely.

reviews.author: Robert Daniels
reviews.text: It feels like we’ve been living in “Seven Days in May” for much of my adult life. My one critique of the film is probably its hopefulness, which now feels like a dream so far removed from our present reality, I felt overcome by anger upon watching it.

reviews.author: Justin Decloux
reviews.text: SEVEN SWORDS is sloppy as hell, but I still think it's a blast. It's difficult for me to pinpoint why one messy Tsui Hark film (because they all are) clicks with me while others are just depressing messes. I guess it's the sweaty commitment to the ideas and their execution? I find SEVEN SWORD beautifully creative, even as I watch a hundred plots faceplant and characters are left in the dust. Seven is too many swords! But even if I'm aware of the negative, and the whole doesn't work, moments still shine for me, and no one could do a Wuxia film like Tsui Hark.

reviews.text: Joe Pevney’s San Fran noir is a showcase for Howard Duff’s Patrick Bateman-esque journalist (feels very much like a precursor for Jake Gyllenhaal’s media muckraker in NIGHTCRAWLER). What’s interesting is that for all the slimy shit photographer Jack Early pulls to get that perfect shot for the newspaper front page, all the double and triple crossing he pulls with the mob families he’s playing, you can’t help but like the guy. It’s a great sociopath character piece and always satisfying to watch a character work all the angles with a “Give NO fucks” attitude. Love seeing younger Lawrence Tierney chomp scenery as one of the mob bosses and Peggy Dow is earnestly The print showed at the New Bev last night was absolutely gorgeous. Funny & dark with a “killer” ending that plays like a metaphor for doing anything to get the shot (for money? For art?), it’s an entertaining ride for sure.

reviews.author: mumblecorgi
reviews.text: Shakedown is an interesting and severely overlooked film noir that, in some ways, beats Wilder's Ace in the Hole, Kazan's A Face in the Crowd, and Gilroy's Nightcrawler to the punch. Even if it's not as great as those movies, Shakedown has some very good things going for it. It is a cautionary tale about blind ambition, the kind of movie they don't really make anymore (even Nightcrawler, which treads in this terrain, makes its case way too subtly, i.e. satirically). It is about a fledgling photography (Howard Duff) who, through a combination of luck, skill, and devious guile, happens to get great, timely news photos. He has also learned that "art" doesn't pay the bills. He works his way…

reviews.text: “Sicario: Day of the Soldado” is a mean fucking movie. That’s sort of its thing. Much like the previous installment of this unlikely franchise, the film drapes itself in darkness so that it can focus our attention on any stray specks of light; one early shot, in which the white halo of a helicopter spotlight tracks a brown man as he sprints towards the Texas border during the dead of night, provides a convenient visual metaphor.

reviews.author: matt lynch
reviews.text: For most of its length a suitably ostentstiously gnarly take on collateral damage from conflicts we engineered for ourselves. Completely lacking in subtlety or even much nuance, sure, but also as unflinching as its predecessor as far as the grim realities at the intersection of clandestine state-sponsored warfare, narcotraffic and its economics, and the self-justification of violence, giving you almost nothing to hold onto except the inevitability of a hopelessly corrupt system continuing to perpetuate itself. Then it obnoxiously tries to grow a moral compass in the last 15 minutes. Don't fucking do that, guys, none of us wears it so well.

reviews.author: Steve Lovecraft
reviews.text: Within the first 10 minutes of Hitman: Dia del Soldier, the sequel immediately sets itself politically antithetical to Sicario. The film opens with a text explaining that there are thousands of people smuggled across the U.S.-Mexico border for profit by Mexican Drug cartels. It then proceeds to show multiple jihadists blowing themselves up in Kansas City (where I was coincidentally watching the film) because, what better way to prove your Islamic extremist point than by smuggling across the border and traveling 1000 miles to blow yourself up at a Dillons? This all helps the cartels, of course, because once you hear about a terror attack you immediately want to do a line of coke.

Because of that opening, I was down with this for a bit, and because it at least seemed to admit that the characters Sheridan meant to be repulsive in the first one (and overt stand-ins for the moral rot brought on by American imperialism and xenophobia) were actually the most alluring. A deeply troubling but not uninteresting sentiment that isn't helped by the fact that both are played by very magnetic…

reviews.author: Matt Singer
reviews.text: Josh Brolin gets one of the all-time great introductions in Sicario. We meet his character, Matt Graver, in a Department of Justice conference room. Everyone else around the table is in a suit and tie; he’s wearing a T-shirt and an unbuttoned collared shirt. He peers at Emily Blunt from over the top of a pair of reading glasses. Brolin placidly asks a series of innocent questions of Blunt’s character, who has just survived a hellish assault on a drug cartel safe house. Blunt leaves then glances down: Graver is conducting national security business in a pair of flip flops, like a reformed hippie who stumbled into a government job.

Marlow Barkley stars as Nemo who’s father (KyleChandler) has tragically passed away, with only her estranged uncle Phillip (Chris O’Dowd) left to raise her. Desperate to see her father again, even if only in dreams, in Slumberland she befriends an outlaw thief (Jason Momoa) and together they traverse varying dreamscapes in search of a fabled treasure thought to grant wishes. Momoa very nearly goes full Jack Sparrow in this swashbuckling adventure, but for the most part it works pretty well. The more poignant moments actually happen between Barkley and O’Dowd as they each process their own grief. Slumberland definitely relies heavily on CG effects, but there’s a vibrance and sparkle…

reviews.author: Sam
reviews.text: Sounder is the one of the only non-romance films that I’ve seen that is thoroughly about love. The saying “it was a labor of love” really reminds me of this film. It tells the story of an African-American family of farmers or sharecroppers living in Louisiana in the 1930s. After the father Nathan (Paul Winfield) is accused of committing a crime, he gets sent away to prison and eventually a labor camp. While he is away from the family, the mother named Rebecca (Cicely Tyson) and the son named David (Kevin Hooks) feel empty and as if they need to be with Nathan. After looking and finding out where Nathan exactly was, Rebecca sends David to go find his father…

reviews.author: Vince The Cinephile
reviews.text: In honor of Ms. Cicely Tyson’s passing, I have decided to look back on her only Oscar-nominated role as Rebecca Morgan in Martin Ritt’s modestly scaled American pastoral drama Sounder. The film follows a poverty-stricken sharecropping Black family during the Great Depression. When their patriarch got arrested for stealing food, Rebecca and her children are left with the burden to survive while eagerly waiting for his return. Ritt (a White director) focuses the Morgan family in such unsentimental and profound outlook where there are no traces of easy morality servings or melodrama.

reviews.author: Filipe Furtado
reviews.text: Ritt treats the material with careful restraint, he avoids the easier sentimental traps childhood memory films can fall into while careful sidestepping the prestige showboating that can come with it. Sounder can feel a bit too guarded on those efforts, the work of very tasteful artists that pushes the family journey into a narrow lane. It is a hard balance that the movie doesn’t always win, but allow for some well earned moving moments. Beyond anything else, Tyson and Winfield performances are very good, whatever the movie risks faulting, they are there to pick things up.

reviews.text: It's about a family, the members of which all love each other. And that's ... about it. There's nothing wrong with simple stories, but it's remarkable how little happens in this movie, about a black share-cropping family in 1930s Louisiana. The father gets arrested for stealing some food and is sent off to a labor camp somewhere. The oldest boy sets off on foot to find him, I guess so he can just say hi, but doesn't find him and comes back home. A few days later the father is released and comes home too, and everybody is happy. Then the oldest boy goes off to school. That's it.

reviews.author: Nick Davis
reviews.text: Sounder remains an American watershed, as touching and sobering, as mature and as kid-friendly, as uplifting and as cautionary as it's always been. Cicely Tyson is of course unsurpassable, but Paul Winfield and especially young Kevin Hooks, who's really the lead, are also exquisite. Martin Ritt could not have directed it with greater sensitivity or poignant restraint, including in his sparing use of music, though when Taj Mahal's voice occasionally alights on a scene, you feel all the more immersed in a rural parish in 1933 Louisiana, and all the more acculturated into this family's life world without presuming to be one of them. Even the fucking dog gives a sensational performance.

reviews.author: fuguette
reviews.text: I love the queerness of this horror. It takes the lost, fragile, between-worlds psychic sylph and makes her a feminine boy haunted by a Victorian gothic past, hounded by sexual hysteria usually associated with the glassy beauty of confused, tender nymphets. He's sexually stunted, Oedpially oppressed, innocent and full-lipped, powerless and passive to his abilities, but still referred to as dangerous and "at a difficult age," just as girls become threatened and threatening when they begin to reach sexual maturity. This subversion of tropes causes a strain of conflict and perversion to run through the whole thing—queerness and sexual deviancy as ostracized other-worldness.
