reviews.text: This is an enigma, yall. Stigma is advanced viewing for fans of Italian horror/eurohorror, an offputting semicollage of trauma and discomfort that constantly threatens to careen off the edge of sanity and stop making sense altogether. You’ll have to dig through really bad acting and dubbing, awful sound mixing, and an extremely nonlinear story, but for patient viewers, there’s a lot to appreciate here.

reviews.author: Klon
reviews.text: Imagine a brooding creep that can kill just by being creepy. Sebastian is a young misogynist that can wish people dead (or sometimes just shove them off of tall buildings), his brooding winds up knocking off a few family members and local girls. He is hypnotised and discovers that in a past life he was even creepier. This is a head trip movie driven by dreams and visions, allowing Larraz to fit in some visionary images amongst the drifting story. Despite the incest and axe murders, this wasn’t as much fun as Larraz’s goat fucking Black Candles.

reviews.author: Stefano Monteforte
reviews.text: A supernatural swing-and-miss from the guy who gave you top shelf genre fare like Vampyres (1974) and Black Candles (1982); an incoherent dollar store pegwarmer mash up of the more boring aspects of The Omen (1976) and every 1970's psychokinesis movie ever made. Christian Borromeo, who you'll remember as David Hess' punching bag in Deodato's The House on the Edge of the Park (1979), the lead here, looks just as bewildered as I was as he sleepwalks through dual roles sending a young girl to a nosebleed tower flopper-death, huffing his mother's (Helga Liné) drawers, duking his sister, and hatcheting up the family in a jealous rage. He mindkills his brother off the road in a firey crash, which causes his girlfriend (Alexandra Bastedo) and her psychic chum to sniff around, trying to unlock the troubled young man's dark secrets, which are still more well-lit than some of this lethargic, flat scareless mutt.

reviews.author: Hollie Horror
reviews.text: Clairvoyance as a curse, a boy born with a veil over his face making him different, making him dangerous as José Ramón Larraz [Symptoms, Edge of the Axe] tries his hand at his very own version of Patrick (1978). Instead of spitting like Patrick, Stigma's Sebastian's lip bleeds and simultaneously a person who has upset him meets their untimely demise. Life after life, incest after incest, movie after movie.

reviews.author: James Grimmer
reviews.text: The sense of loss and the impact that death causes can't be predicted, nor can they be ignored. In fact, they are part and parcel of Sebastian's adjustment to his circumstances as well as the pathological fears and hallucinations that he experiences; thus, the question of whether he is able to control his thoughts couldn't be more weighty. It is one of many points of interest, along with a revealing hypnosis session, a house that was built over an old cemetery, tension between brothers, and a hatred so strong that it causes people to die. It's a very unusual state of affairs. It's dreamlike at times but also mysterious. If that doesn't pique your interest, I don't know what will.…

reviews.author: Blake Bergman "Various Spaghetti"
reviews.text: "Strike of the Panther" is a 1989 action film directed by Brian Trenchard-Smith. A sequel to "Day of the Panther" (1988), it continues the story of Jason Blade from the film before, even complete with an inserted prologue at the beginning of the film using a complete montage of scenes from the first film recanting the story with voiceover narration. It's a trope that I see a lot in Full Moon movies in easy recognition, but really, it's a staple of direct to video sequels that as much as they seem like a copout to a degree to fill time, it now is nostalgic piece of charm in retrospect that reminds me when these films were prevalent. Trenchard-Smith eventually became…

He beats up goons, gets his leg humped by a tiny man in lederhosen while being chased by a whip-wielding dominatrix, and accidentally walks in on a barking man in a chicken costume. This stuff is great; exactly that kind of material that made Day of the Panther so great and memorable. We even get an awkward Flashdance montage between Blade and his girlfriend from the first movie. This is classic stuff here, people!

reviews.text: 'Super Duper Alice Cooper' is an interesting look at the Alice Cooper phenomenon during the 70s and early 80s, featuring some great early concert footage and a fun narrative (I loved the use of a silent horror film as a framing device). Rather than doing a talking head documentary, the interview subjects only appear in voice form, and it was nice to hear statements by everybody from Elton John to Johnny Rotten and Dee Snider. I would probably consider myself more of a casual fan of Alice Cooper and most familiar with his 80s and early 90s output, so this was a great look into that earlier period and a reminder that I need more of the 70s albums. Even though I really enjoyed this, I wish it would have gone on a bit longer to show his rise back to mainstream fame with the 80s comeback and beyond.

reviews.author: jryn7
reviews.text: So my journey through the Swordsman Trilogy ends with watching the original for the first time. Tsui Hark was a huge fan of the legendary King Hu, and Swordsman was Tsui’s attempt to bring Hu back to Hong Kong filmmaking after his work in Taiwan dried up, with an adaptation of a famous book by Jin Yong. Probably unsurprisingly, the two control freaks could not coexist, and depending on the story Hu either quit or was fired, and Tsui and frequent collaborator Ching Siu-tung took over. Hu still gets a directing credit anyway, but percentage-wise this feels 99% Tsui and Ching’s work.

reviews.author: mayhemperez
reviews.text: For a movie that allegedly was first helmed by King Hu and then handled by a myriad of directors selected by Tsui Hark (who was the producer) after Hu dropped out, its surprisingly cohesive. It works in its favor actually, giving the movie its own unique identity, something that incorporates elements from all the directors involved. I dont know all of these, but i did recognise King Hu's whimsical vibe, Ching Siu-Tung's madcap wirework-fueled action choreography and unfortunately, Tsui Hark's penchant for storytelling becoming disjointed by the end. But regardless, its production was still a mess and it shows. In the end, its not that memorable of a movie, but its an interesting experiment worth seeing if you consider yourself a real wuxia fan. And also because the sequel is apparently a classic and i guess you should have some context for that one (i'm watching it sometime this month, can't wait).

reviews.author: sakana1
reviews.text: Perhaps the most powerful thing about Symptoms is the way it renders the familiar unfamiliar. The film takes place within a very limited range of settings, with the great majority of it restricted to the house and the river, as well as its immediate surroundings. We come to know those places efficiently and comfortably, aided by the rhythmic return to the sound and image of a rowboat cutting through the river's water, and the recognizable rooms and angles in the home. Even the unsettling, recurring shot of the steep steps up the attic quickly becomes familiar, associated with night, sleeplessness, and uncertainty.

reviews.text: (Ultimately, the tension comes from sympathizing with Hannah so much and not wanting her to be hurt in any way. It's a grey sort of sympathy, obviously, but what she is up against is exploitation and isolation. I relate a little too much to the latter part and we all live under the yoke of exploitation. That this is presented in warmly autumnal hues and British country shadows suffuses this with an atmosphere that speaks of folk horror while at no point really engaging in traditional folk horror trappings. It simply wears the highlights of it, the scent of it. The psychological drama at the core of this is part thriller part slasher; the combination of flavors makes this a pleasing experience.)

reviews.author: Jamelle Bouie
reviews.text: As one of the inmates points out, there is nothing about this particular prison that is unique. Inmates across the country live in similar or worse conditions. Our prison system is, on the whole, a nightmare of cruelty and brutality. And the harsh truth is that this is what millions of Americans want, as evidenced by the way we joke, the way we vote, and the way we don’t care to do anything differently. Americans might be more secular than we’ve ever been but we’re no less Puritan, and with that comes the perverse belief that everyone, the condemned and the “elect” alike, gets what they deserve.

reviews.author: Will Sloan
reviews.text: Welcome to the Bruno Mattei version of The Irishman. Shockingly inept, full of baffling storytelling, editing, and directorial choices. The first 10-or-so minutes are as disorienting as A Night to Dismember as it zips through about 40 years of historical detail and character relations before arriving at what in any normal movie would be Act 3. It’s impossible to tell what Levinson and Co. expect us to feel about these characters, their relationships, and their milieu, except that they seem to think the protagonist, crime boss of bosses Frank Costello, is basically a good guy. They come nowhere close to building that case.

It might be the best deaths in horror movies, the steamiest scenes from erotic thrillers, or in this case, a compilation of martial arts fight scenes with John Saxon sleepily narrating the clips. reviews.author: Filipe Furtado
reviews.text: Brutal and very downbeat. Great location work and does a great job of making the world feel increasingly tight around Ventura. The movie is animated by the tension of his justified paranoia and attachments. He keeps losing this and getting more violent as a reaction. And there’s Belmondo as his new contact, their scenes together are so wonderful, a warmth in such a doomed movie. The two actors are near their best, and as Belmondo shot it just after Breathless, he is charismatic but also in his last not quite movie star part. Claude Sautet directed, he would get much more personal with time, but I don’t think he has anything else this controlled.

reviews.author: J
reviews.text: In this minefield of hide and seek, the cruel command of time gradually wilts power and allies. Tried in absentia, wanted criminal-on-the-run Abel grazes against the law after a holdup and getaway gone wrong. He flees from Italy—his personal casualties in exchange for escape lay awash on French shores—counting on his cronies’ protection. Hard times reveal true friends, however. And in the code of the gangster, a friend is only a friend when a friend is of use. Forsaken, Abel gains sympathy from Éric instead, a young criminal who works for himself and eventually helps conceal him from the authorities. Desperation takes hold of Abel as his funds dwindle. He commits more crime to tide himself over with stolen money…

reviews.author: Stephen M
reviews.text: I mainly know Claude Sautet from his character driven films from the 1970s on ("Cesar and Rosalie", "Vincent, Francois, Paul and the Others", "A Heart in Winter"), often about relationships among the middle-class. So what a shocker to learn he'd done a crime film early on! This was quite a good watch. It has many of the features you'd expect in a gangster film. But like Sautet's later works, it too emphasizes the relationships, which made it perfect for me.

reviews.author: Jaime Rebanal 🇵🇸
reviews.text: I hate the English title for this movie that's up on here. Only because the French title, Classe tous risques sounds like "classe touriste," which nails down the themes of this downbeat Claude Sautet movie. It's maybe the most fitting way to make a film all about this criminal lifestyle, especially when the ramifications of your own misdeeds are set to bite you and the people you love at some point. "Classe touriste" simply means "economy class," which hints at how Abel Davos's glory was always short-lived, and trying to assimilate back into society would prove futile for his own life, especially with the threat of death looming around.

reviews.text: Boldly asserts itself as the true conduit of Mary Shelley’s unrealized feminist vision, only to illustrate the kind of shallow, contradictory feminism embodied by president Barbie dolls. Undoubtedly, a film that takes big swings which I appreciate in a landscape that prioritizes shareholder profits, but big swings sometimes result in a strike out just the same. I think the lesson here is that genre films really deserve more respect for being incredibly difficult to do well. Dare I say, far more difficult than your average prestige drama. A baffling film all around and surprisingly dull to boot. Feels like it got hacked to pieces in the reshoots and edits. Maybe there’s a coherent, satisfying version somewhere in the ether, but honestly, I kinda doubt it.

reviews.text: Maybe it speaks to the kind of weird ass wuxia I've seen in the past that I didn't find this one particularly out there, despite the presence of demonic cult leader fused at the back to his maniacal sister. It comes down firmly in the camp (and there's a LOT of camp) of romantic fantasy; other than the gravity-defying antics of the martial brothers and sisters of the Eight Sects, it shies away from the exotic black magic batshittery the 80s brought. For this is a 90s movie; the 90s writ large in billowing plumes of dry ice, the hard lines of blue gel lighting and a portentous, orchestral-hit-heavy score. Kind of like a Meatloaf video.

Li Han-hsiang's 1977 Dream of the Red Chamber (an early starring role for Brigitte Lin, seen here at the pinnacle of her career) similarly revels in tragedy, spending most of its final half on just a few scenes as the lovers lament the forces that have led to their…

Dazu fühlt sich die Lovestory von Cheung und Lin zwar leidenschaftlich, aber nie wirklich überzeugend an, was auch übertragbar auf die Kämpfe ist: viel Elan, reichlich spritzendes Blut, aber auch viele schnelle Schnitte und Step Printing, um den relativen Mangel an Skills zu kaschieren. reviews.author: Lou (rhymes with wow!)
reviews.text: Tsui Hark's debut film was a bit less impactful for me on this revisit, sadly enough. I do love the idea of a wuxia with Euro horror/Giallo influences, but the movie plays out in such a convoluted fashion, that it takes away from the experience. The atmosphere is great and there is still some fun martial arts on display here (which is elevated by Tsui's keen eye for framing and lighting a scene), but don't expect the story to make much sense.

reviews.author: laird
reviews.text: Going in only knowing that this was Tsui Hark's first film, I was kind of unprepared for just how strange it is. First off, the title isn't poetic like a giallo (Blood Stained Butterfly, Lizard in a Woman's Skin, etc), but literal. There are killer butterflies in this movie. Secondly, it has a tone/mood I haven't seen in other Tsui Hark films, more akin to Gothic or Euro-horror: a dream-like quality that shifts to nightmarish as things become more outlandish and horrific. Then a murder mystery unfolds as mystical kung-fu masters (collectively known as The Thunders) gather in a spooky castle with Tien (leader of the Ten Flags), Green Shadow (a rogue female martial arts master), and Fong the scholar.…

In The Butterfly Murders Tsui blends wuxia, mystery, and the possibility of the supernatural - all in a typically crazy plot. Master Shum (Chang Kuo-chu) writes to a group of people to come help him and his wife at his castle: martial arts scholar Fong (Lau Siu Ming), the leader of the “#3 ranked” clan Tien Lung (Wong Shu-tong, looking like Iron Chef or a Bruce Lee villain) and his clan, and wildcard swordswoman Green Shadow (Michelle Yim). reviews.author: Jake Cole
reviews.text: To be honest I'm still not sure what the plot is even after the protagonist explains everything about 10 minutes before the end. But who could possibly care when Tsui announces himself with a debut that blends the most outré edges of wuxia with the sleek, confounding style of giallo? Even in the ghastly quality rip I watched, the dreamy, queasy colors and distortions of the cinematography shine through, as does Tsui's modern approach to action framing and cutting that emphasizes the confusion of jumbled close-ups to capture the half-absurd, half-oddly terrifying threat of lethally poisoning butterflies swarming unsuspecting warriors. That the ostensible lead literally walks out of the movie after he solves things and leaves the rest to a brutal climactic fight without him is just the final hilarious, exuberant quirk in an outstanding debut.

reviews.text: Supremely entertaining mash-up of soccer and martial arts from the director of "In the Line of Duty III," featuring Yuen Biao at the height of his athletic prowess. This packs a whole hell of a lot of movie into less than 90 minutes! It's been awhile since I've seen "Shaolin Soccer," but this film focuses more on soccer club politics than what I remember of Stephen Chow's hit (and also features a hyper-violent "Police Story"-esque fight that comes out of nowhere and leaves at least one stuntman engulfed in flames). This might be the first time I've watched a film and felt like it was playing at 1.5 speed: the pace is truly dizzying and a new gag is tossed at the viewer every 30 seconds. "The Champions" is basically a live-action cartoon. Highly recommended for fans of Hong Kong action-comedies.

reviews.author: jrhovind
reviews.text: As hyperkinetically dazzling as any of his wuxia films, Hark goes to the kitchen to imagine a kind of martial arts comedy with chef’s knives and pans; physical dedication and spiritual enlightenment the interwoven essential paths toward pulling off one perfect feast. As with the Once Upon a Time saga, the real danger seems to be the homogenizing effects of an enforced corporatized globalization (“Cuisine is the kingdom of the Chinese. I want to conquer it bit by bit”); against the threat of a thuggish conglomerate and his dreams of flattening everything until there’s nothing left but profit, a few scrappy underdogs and has-beens finding it within themselves to imagine a way of maintaining the local integrity of their sensory lives.

reviews.text: It’s not about the destination, but the journey; even more so, the people you get to spend it with. Unapologetically Irish. I feckin loved it, naturally. Captures our jet-black witticisms and half-baked sardony to an absolute tee. It can’t hurt, then, that the tunes all bang and its depiction of working class solidarity is as contagiously congenial as it comes. I love Sing Street. But theres no Sing Street without The Commitments. Honest, over-stuffed with soul, with a spirit so infectiously Dublin-bred you’ll not see fit to sit still. Almost fantastical, until it’s not. As if it exists in its own world, rules and all. And honestly? Any world with The Commitments is one I’d do bad things to be a part of.

reviews.author: Paul Elliott
reviews.text: This splendidly constructed war movie from Around the World in 80 Days director Michael Anderson is an account of the historical Operation Chastise, and the destruction of German hydroelectric dams during WWII. The script is an amalgamation of two novels, Guy Gibson’s Enemy Coast Ahead (1946) and Paul Brickhill’s The Dam Busters (1951), and it generates some solid performances to blend with the exquisite cinematography and the iconic theme by Eric Coates. It's very much a product of its time however as no observations are given to the estimated death of over 1,600 civilians, more than 1,000 of which turned out to be forced labour camp inmates and prisoners of war; which subsequently lead to Article 56 of the Protocol I amendment to the Geneva Conventions, outlawing attacks on dams.

reviews.text: Tally ho,chaps! The stiffest of stiff-upper-lips..not to mention some splendid mustaches..are on display as Richard Todd leads his elite squadron of bombers on a top-secret mission to cripple Nazi Germanys war machine by taking out two critical hydro-electric dams! The mission is the brainchild of eccentric engineer Barnes Wallis, wonderfully played by Michael Redgrave, who designs the revolutionary 'bouncing bombs' needed to breach the dams defences! We won't dwell on the infamous and ever-so-slightly problematic question of the 'Dam Busters dog'..get over it, it's a 70 year old film,cut it a bit of slack..and instead move swiftly on to the climactic raid which is still a terrific action sequence despite some understandably very dated FX work! Much is made of George Lucas's debt to Kurosawa and 'Hidden Fortress' for 'Star Wars' but it could be argued 'The Dam Busters' was just as much in his thoughts when planning 'Star Wars' climactic bombing run on the Death Star! Chocks away!

reviews.author: ℛℴ𝒹𝓃ℯ𝓎 🔵🟡
reviews.text: Richard Harris’s Bull McCabe isn’t just a man obsessed with a patch of Irish land — he’s a generational curse in human form. You see it most cruelly in his son, Tadgh, a man so brow-beaten he barely exists beyond a dim echo of who he might have become. He’s like a ghost of a child who stopped developing the day his father decided fear was more useful than love. Now he drifts through life as a walking contagion, infecting every moment with silent rage. You won’t get joy or kindness from Tadgh, only pain. Watching him is like peering into a private hell sculpted over a lifetime of abuse.

reviews.text: Excellent acting from an impressive cast. It has a powerful premise regarding eternal issues bound to create everlasting conflict: the pitfalls of pride, holding on to historical & family traumas and in acquiring land at all costs. Highly emotive matters, which will sadly and unfortunately continue to bring out the very worst in people for as long as we are on earth. This expertly brings all those contentious and explosive subjects to the fore and it leaves the viewer with a lot to ponder on afterwards. I don't think Richard Harris was ever better in his entire career; a truly superb performance.

reviews.text: Released a year after the abolition of the House Un-American Activities Committee, The Front is the first Hollywood film to tackle the trauma of McCarthyism head-on, breaking a long collective silence. More than just a historical reconstruction, the film is a civil testimony, deeply rooted in the past of its authors. Martin Ritt and screenwriter Walter Bernstein were both victims of Senator McCarthy's ideological persecution, and this direct experience gives the film a rare authenticity that emerges in its portrayal of the daily lives of those who, in order to continue working, were forced to hide their talent behind the anonymity of “front men”, a practice that was sadly common at the time. The film operates on multiple semantic levels,…

reviews.author: Slig001
reviews.text: The Front is set during the 'McCarthy era' and ensuing Hollywood blacklist, which was a secretive list of names banned from working in the industry due to suspected links to the Communist Party. Sort of like the low tech version of being shadowbanned on Twitter. The film focuses on Woody Allen's cashier who gets a break when offered the chance to "front" for his blacklisted writer friend. The Front takes a serious subject and constructs a fun and entertaining drama around it, with Woody Allen providing most of the jokes. The film exposes the total nonsense of the whole situation - studios having to pass up good work, while exceptional talent is left on the sidelines for spurious reasons. The…

reviews.text: The Girl with a Bracelet is perhaps the single film I have seen that best captures the experience of the juror during a criminal trial. As someone who has spent his fair share of time around American courtrooms, I cannot recall a movie so committed to the gradual unfurling of evidence that helps to present a case to a jury. Each witness brings new bits of information to the table to help complete a picture of the circumstances surrounding an alleged crime – motive, sexual history, upbringing all help to create a cohesive mosaic effect in director Stephane Demoustier’s whip smart legal drama.

When Jeannette Walls, the real woman, chooses to forgive her abusive father, that is her choice entirely. When Jeannette Walls, the character, chooses to forgive her father, it sends a troubling message.

This movie blends comedy and drama together perfectly and the film has several scenes that nearly brought a tear to my eye. I can't stress this enough though Sam Elliot is phenomenal, this is the best performance I've ever seen from him and I couldn't see anyone else playing this part better than he did. The scene where he's reading lines for a script might just be some of the finest acting I've ever seen in a movie. I really hope more people check this out soon, we hopefully have our first lock for Best Actor.

The movie never really goes into the flashbacks of his mistaken-filled past, only that he wants to reconcile his relationships with his ex-wife (real-life wife Katharine Ross—as a Ross fanatic I wanted more than just two scenes with her!) and estranged daughter (Krysten Ritter); Elliott deftly hints at the inner demons lurking without having to pronounce specifically what they are. reviews.author: Lexzilla
reviews.text: When this opened with a rape scene, I did think ‘urgh’. But happily, a few minutes later, all the perpetrators were dead and the film turned out not to be a horrible sleaze-fest of sexual assault, but instead an entertaining sleaze-lite-fest of pulpy grieving revenge. Directed by Teruo Ishii, returning from a long filmmaking hiatus, this one follows a guy who takes on two yakuza families after his fiancé gets killed in their cross crossfire. While it does kind of play out predictably, there a certain madcap flair to some of the directing choices and both less violence and more nudity than you would expect. It’s not mind-blowing, but it is an enjoyable enough way to pass ninety minutes.

reviews.author: Jon Peters
reviews.text: A self-proclaimed “veteran crank”, Teruo Ishii spent his 1980s in television, according to Chris D. in his book Outlaw Masters of Japanese Film, “due to the downturn in Japanese movie production Ishii worked mostly in television in the eighties, finally directing a yakuza picture again in 1991”. That yakuza picture is THE HITMAN: BLOOD SMELLS LIKE ROSES (Za Hittoman: Chi wa bara no nioi, 1991) which marked his first feature since VIOLENT WARRIOR (Boryoku senshi, 1979), but the decade-long absence of between films showed no signs of any technique rust, as the film is within his sadistic excesses from his peak period at Nikkatsu, this V-cinema production that “curdles into something strange and idiosyncratic”, writes Jake Cole of Slant Magazine.…

reviews.author: Gregor Kreyca
reviews.text: Cult director and exploitation mad-man Teruo Ishii returned after a 12 year hiatus to the directing chair to make this little Neo-Noir action/revenge V-Cinema flick. It certainly does not compare to his best work in the late 60’s to the mid 70’s. Neither visually nor when it comes to energy and inventiveness. But for a V-Cinema production I think this was quite decent. Slow-paced but short with some visual flair, some solid action, bursts of violence and a more then healthy amount of sex and nudity.

However, the pacing of the film is inconsistent, switching between different plot lines. One involves the love/hate triangle between Muller, his associate played by Richard Arlen, and Muller’s young ward played by Vera Hrubá Ralston, formerly a champion Czech figure skater. reviews.text: Nice piece of documentary filmmaking that feels immersive and has more of a fly-on-the-wall quality rather than necessarily trying to get a narrative point across. It was nice to see that this didn’t turn into a slumming “Look how these weird rural people live” kind of a doc; there were some very nice everyday moments with the Long Island locals for whom this track is a part of their lives. You’re not getting any history about stock car racing in America or any narration directing you to a particular emotional state of mind, you’re just dropping into a small slice of life and checking out what’s going on there.

reviews.text: By adding different layers to a well-known Chinese folklore, Tsui Hark manages to elevate it to an experience encompassing queer, political, and cinematic spectrums. Unlike Green Snake, in which theatricality comes at the cost of sincerity, The Lovers features the true flesh and blood of two human beings, transcending gender, class, or any other man-made barriers.

reviews.author: Lou (rhymes with wow!)
reviews.text: Definitely the most mellow and romantic Tsui Hark movie I have seen to date. Probably the most aesthetically pleasing one as well. The Lovers has its silly moments, but luckily it never becomes a comedy. On the contrary, it slowly but surely moves into (melo)drama territory, especially in its downer third act.

reviews.author: Sean Gilman
reviews.text: Starts as your typical guy-falls-in-love-with-girl-dressed-as-a-guy rom-com, then turns into hallucinatory elemental melodrama. Skies of pink, purple and orange; tears of blood; fierce winds and rain erasing the unnatural constraints of the social order; the earth swallowing the lovers whole.

reviews.author: Shea
reviews.text: Not Tsui's most formally audacious - indeed the most sedate and gentle I have seen him - but for me he excels at romance and this is one of the great love stories, after all, so of course I couldn't help but fall completely for it. Despite being made 30 years earlier, The Love Eterne is a little more daringly Gender, but Tsui more than matches the visual artistry and the particular brand of sweetness he (along with Charlie and Nicky, of course) brings to the first half makes the finale just as effective. Love the songs so much. Love Charlie Yeung so much.

reviews.author: Augie
reviews.text: In my eyes, the magic of cinema lies in its delicate relationship with hopes and dreams---and here my hopes and dreams became intertwined with those of the characters. Just like with the Love Eterne, it's as though I'm seeing my dreams in these images, I'm seeing my dreams unfold before me. If The Love Eterne was my arrival at the top of a mountain in the clouds, then with The Lovers here I am surrounded by clouds and flowers, overcome with love, I have learned how to dance with the butterflies---I have learned how to dream with the butterflies. Who knows what tomorrow may bring? Will my dreams become reality? For now, it doesn't matter. What matters is that today I have found peace, today I have found love. I have found these things by letting my dreams flow into cinema, and by letting cinema flow into my dreams.

reviews.author: Avirup
reviews.text: Starts off as sweet and goofy romcom with Charlie Yeung and Nicky Wu having the most lovely chemistry, then it turns into a truly glorious melodrama where the societal reality strikes. Tsui makes this transition remarkably and the images become otherworldly almost. The ending is just marvelous, it's like forces of nature helping love conquer, it's inevitably tragic and painful but also incredibly beautiful at the same time.

reviews.text: Probably one of Tsui Hark's most beautiful movies that I've seen thus far. But in that same area, it's also maybe he saddest film that I think I'd seen from him, perhaps owing to how The Lovers starts out, before the sudden shift in tone towards ethereal melodrama in its second half. Not only is it always so enthralling, but in how it interrogates the social restrictions which ultimately keep these two lovers separate from one another. Of course, being an adaptation of the classic Chinese story "Butterfly Lovers," one can only sense that the happiness we're feeling is as strong as it can ever be, before we know the inevitable doom its two leads will eventually meet.

reviews.author: AJ
reviews.text: The Lovers starts as a typical, light-hearted guy, Shan-pak, who falls in love with a girl dressed as a guy, Ying-tai, at school. The atmosphere is endlessly enjoyable, the chemistry is otherworldly, and the lovers exist in their own universe. After 6 months, Ying-tai returns home to her arranged marriage despite any and all pleas of marrying Shan-pak. The tenants of nature rebel against societal powers, and tears of blood lead to bursts of wind and torrents of rain. The universe sets straight elemental forces. Love conquers.

reviews.text: The dark, serious looking poster on here is very misleading; this is a colorful, goofy movie. Unfortunately, it gets bogged down by overplotting what should be a simple story of one student trying to kill his master while another student tries to save him. There's also too many random subplots such as local thugs that follow Jet Li around begging him to train them and a bank foreclosing on his master's shop. This all leads to a lack of fight scenes. The fight scenes we do get are great though including an awesome rooftop finale. Aside from wishing for more fight scenes, it's a very likeable movie with a charmingly cheesy 90s aesthetic.

Johnny owns his own brand of kung fu schools, seeking to defeat all the masters in America before heading to Hong Kong. Just as Johnny is about to kill Tak, he is saved by Anna, who takes him to her camper outside the city.

reviews.text: A quick look at a low level Montreal mob member. He tries to move up and gets smacked down. So he decides to spill the beans on public radio. I feel it helps because when it does happen. It stands out. Like I said, this is a quick look. The film is just under 90 minutes. It goes by fast with the grit you expect from a film about the mob. No matter where they are found. The main character is not exactly likeable but neither are the "good guys". Everyone seems to be out to get what they can. Such is the world. Even in 1975.

reviews.text: Park Chan-wook's debut is the kind of film you desperately wanna turn off ten minutes in, but then recall you can't because your masochism drives you to canon completion and self-hatred. There's a familiar pattern I've learned that comes with this mindset: I'll spend a considerable amount of time hunting down a title I know will be bald, but proceed with the process anyway because the obsession will not tolerate a single missing piece of the puzzle (at least when it comes to directorial features). Which is why I'm in a bind with his sophomore follow up, TRIO (1997)…does a copy even exist anywhere? If so, please send details. I'd like to continue punishing myself.

reviews.author: anna nomaly
reviews.text: The script is messy and often dramatically inert, swooning and brooding over a love triangle that never takes off, but Park comes out of the gate with a cogent vision of his own style, obviously knowledgeable about crime cinema the world over and particularly keyed into this specific cultural moment of fresh auteurist voices honing their genre obsessions into something personal. While the photoshoot milieu of the opening passages feels more keenly-observed than the gangster material, the story’s inevitable crescendos of violence give him plenty of room to practice and flex his budding directorial muscles, lingering on indelible visual moments like the extended elevator kiss and inspiring some appropriately haunted performances from his actors. Although we get to know the situation much more than we actually get to know the characters, it’s pretty clear throughout that we’re getting to know Park. Given the timing, fellow Blankies will undoubtedly scream when silent film briefly takes center stage.

reviews.author: Dan McCoy
reviews.text: Montage as film criticism. Montage as cultural satire. Montage as vehicle for big laffs. And, ultimately, as a way of constructing a cockeyed, MAD Magazine landscape of America circa 1933 - 1969. Even when the Movie Orgy is tedious (and, in the 4.75 hours-ish version I saw -- which is one of the shorter cuts, from what I understand -- it would be hard not to be tedious once in a while)... even then the tediousness seems to be part of the strategy, whether it's letting you zone out before delivering the punch, or whether it's by making the tediousness part of the joke (the endless stream of plausible "last" clips at the finale).

reviews.text: Really an uncanny act of brilliance, that while I've seen others like it now, (obviously like the AGFA Mixtapes) really was stand alone when it was made in 1968. Also the runtime felt no existent to me which is insane as its pushing 5 hours long. Obviously great to watch straight forward, future views of this film just might make it a cinephiles best cure for insomnia as I can also see going forward that this is a marathon that you put on as you go to bed. Each segment is well placed dosages of television and pop culture yesteryear, almost like scrolling Youtube for clips and finding something interesting with each click.

reviews.author: Darren Carver-Balsiger
reviews.text: The Movie Orgy is a movie of movies. It is a collage of culture and cinema. Its spine is formed by footage from various B-movies, but cartoons, adverts, and television clips also feature prominently. Despite its extreme runtime The Movie Orgy is never really boring. It's a montage of joy, celebrating popular culture and cutting things together in a fun way. There are moments where the Vietnam War and Richard Nixon are targeted for satire, but mostly the film is a lovable tribute to the quirks of mid-century Americana. It's a fascinating document of history, unintentionally collecting cultural artefacts that now paint a portrait of American society at the time. The adverts reveal just how much commercialisation was already a vital part of American culture and how visual mediums would bolster it. The Movie Orgy is an unique and nostalgic ode to pop culture, crafted as one of the most astonishing montages in cinema history. Very lovable.

It's the kind of thing you'd see on a display shelf at the airport and buy for your father, crack open on your flight, fall asleep before finishing the first chapter, and forget to give to your dad after landing. reviews.text: a fascinating, albeit beguiling, case study of a filmmaker giving zero fucks about audience or critical reception and creating something impenetrable and defiant of genre classification; much of The Osterman Weekend’s narrative shortcomings and overall messiness would be easy to attribute to studio tinkering — it was notoriously taken from Peckinpah during editing — but in watching, the admittedly rather different, director’s cut, it’s clear that much of its abstractions and eccentricities are intentional and, if nothing else, only furthered in Peckinpah’s true unfiltered vision; at face value, the surveillance obsessions and espionage elements make this feel like Peckinpah’s The Conversation but this is actually Peckinpah’s The Big Chill — friendship rendered cold and trust weaponized, a vision of yuppies and their transgressions, hangups, fears and acts of violence from a filmmaker who couldn’t care less about the generation to succeed his own

reviews.text: Facsimile of “Rashomon,” and while it has a starting point with pungent black & white cinematography, it nevertheless turns the loaded drama into heavy-handed solemnity which turns into artiness which turns into a ponderous chore for the viewer to sniff out the differences between a Japanese story and a labored Westernized variation. Paul Newman, methodically, disappears into the role of a Mexican bandit rapist but with so much slurring dialogue to chew on it soon becomes an overreaching actor’s assignment. The Outrage, by director Martin Ritt, isn’t some kind of awful outrage of bad entertainment, but it’s like being a jeweler who has the discovery that this one is the fake diamond. Also Laurence Harvey, Edward G. Robinson, William Shatner, and Claire Bloom as “the poor white trash slut.”

The acting is fine with a solid cast but gotta say Paul Newman with a very awkward Mexican visage and accent felt very cringy to watch and a poor utilization of his stature. I know that Rashomon has been done in many stories and was a groundbreaking story arc but seeing it rebuilt in such a familiar fashion kinda gave me an uncanny valley evaluation of the piece that I found offsetting. reviews.author: Paul Anthony Johnson
reviews.text: This remake of Rashomon is an odd muddle of tones, as a premise that necessitates heated, dreamlike intensity and a sustained note of existential dread falls prey to director Martin Ritt's congenital literalism and mawkish humanist piety. Cinematographer James Wong Howe does what he can by alternating sun-bleached clarity with oneiric abstraction, but the cartoonishly overwrought staging and performances undercut any poetic ambiguity. By the final iteration of events, Ritt angles toward outright farce, but because that's not really in his wheelhouse either, the movie just degenerates into a lot of unpleasant mugging.

reviews.text: It goes without saying that Akira Kurosawa is one the most influential filmmakers of all time. His iconic film Rashomon (1950) is recognized as helping Japanese cinema breakthrough into the west after winning the prestigious Golden Lion award at the Venice Film Festival. It is widely known how often Kurosawa’s films get remade in the west such as The Magnificent Seven (1960) and A Fistful of Dollars (1964) for Seven Samurai (1954) and Yojimbo (1961) respectively. Despite following the same general plot of their Japanese counterparts, these two western films manage to justify their existence thanks to strong directorial voices and creative drives. One remake that seems to have gone under the radar from the public eye is Martin Ritt’s…

reviews.author: Japan Society Film
reviews.text: During his lifetime, director Yasujiro Ozu maintained a trove of personal diaries that reveal a remarkably intimate side of the legendary filmmaker. Pulling from essays, home movies, archival photos, and recollections of Ozu-gumi (Ozu staff/collaborators) like Kogo Noda and Kinuyo Tanaka, The Ozu Diaries attempts to unmask the mystique surrounding Ozu’s persona. With fascinating anecdotes—such as Ozu hearing a rumor that Setsuko Hara could not act prior to working with her—and contributions by Kiyoshi Kurosawa and Wim Wenders, The Ozu Diaries offers a glimpse of one of cinema’s greatest masters, an auto portrait told through his own words.

reviews.text: Picture a wave. In the ocean. You can see it, measure it, its height, the way the sunlight refracts when it passes through. And it’s there. And you can see it, you know what it is. It’s a wave. And then it crashes in the shore and it’s gone. But the water is still there. The wave was just a different way for the water to be, for a little while. The wave returns to the ocean, where it came from and where it’s supposed to be.Dear god I absolutely loved this show to death. From its surprisingly brilliant humor, to the ethics and morals it teaches, it’s all beautiful and blended together perfectly to create something unlike most other shows. If you genuinely haven’t seen nor heard of this show, you’re seriously missing out on a potentially masterclass of fiction that became of my personal favorite shows out there.

reviews.text: Yuen Woo-Ping does his own Under Die Hard Siege, and it’s an absolute blast. Everyone either dies horribly (so much indiscriminate innocent death) or gets brutally pummeled, the silly comedy has actual pay-off, and the blistering fights make inventive use of cruise-ship spaces. Woo-Ping cleverly tailors the spectacle to location: a gym, a slippery sauna, the engine room pipe-maze, etc. Kenny Ho makes for a pretty boring McClane but is a pretty fierce fighter; really the only memorable presence is Elaine Lui’s taunting undercover terrorist. Thankfully, this New Years action bash and its murder mayhem compensate for a shortage of characters or plot.

reviews.text: This incredible film explores what effects being haunted by mistakes made and opportunities missed can have on one's life. And it does so in a very well scripted, beautifully directed and superbly acted violent drama. What makes this film so exceptional is that it effortlessly switches between the mundane (it has these wonderful ' slice of life' moments, which show Argentinian culture at its best and worst) and the philosophical. I would spoil too much when I explain the latter, let's just say it explores the human boundaries of compassion and revenge.This is a film any lover of intelligent and intense cinema should watch and if you, like I did, allow yourself to be swept away by it, it will stay with you for a long time.

reviews.author: AD917
reviews.text: Made during a time when Vietnam war epics were at their most popular, The Siege of Firebase Gloria was a throwback to the modestly scaled hard boiled studies of men at war that Hollywood used to produce decades earlier. In that era, this sort of elevated pulp might’ve been directed by Samuel Fuller; in 1989 it fell on the versatile shoulders of Brian Trenchard-Smith.

reviews.author: Daniel Shillito
reviews.text: There are no stirring heroics, no rousing patriotic speeches, and certainly no examination of the conflict's causes or consequences in The Siege of Firebase Gloria—just the cold, efficient butchery skills of men killing other men. There's very little in the way of jingoistic clichés and slo-mo heroics here; the whole film feels more like a leaked military snuff tape with its brutally frank depiction of the war, where both U.S. military personnel and Viet Cong fight tooth and nail as unsympathetic governments on either side move chess pieces about. These are ultimately scared human beings, some barely more than boys, who don't know why they have to do these horrible things, only that they must if they want to survive.…

reviews.author: More_Badass
reviews.text: Gritty decapitation-aplenty Vietnam war flick unabashedly stripped down almost entirely to ‘namsploitation mayhem. R. Lee Ermey is great in a rare lead role alongside an intense Wings Hauser, as the duo and a dwindling platoon weather a Tet Offensive onslaught in the titular base. Robert Arevalo deserves praise too as the VC colonel humanized with as much no-nonsense world-weariness and tactical wherewithal as Ermey’s sergeant. Brian Trenchard-Smith is the real MVP of The Siege of Firebase Gloria; his direction unleashes a near hour straight of combat with chaotic scale, action-dense tracking shots, and goopy squib grisliness. Even though the film is maximized for carnage, the animalistic cruelty that grips characters alongside the boots-on-the-ground battle fatigue, perpetual casualties, and pyrrhic victories among both sides gives this action-packed barnstormer a decidedly anti-war slant.

reviews.text: The Sleeping City is an average film noir bolstered by a few really good choices. Richard Conte goes undercover at a hospital where a shooting has happened, leaving an intern dead. He falls in love with a nurse played by Coleen Gray and befriends an elevator operator played by Richard Taber, though there is more to them than meets the eye. While the story is just okay, there are some really interesting directions it takes to keep it from being forgettable. I really liked the performances, particularly Richard Taber and Coleen Gray. Richard Taber plays Pop Ware very amiable, yet there is an edge to his character. Coleen Gray is always a welcome sight with me, and she is able to work with a lot here. The camera work is really good in this one too, particularly toward the end. While it does take a bit to get going, it ends up being a fairly engaging movie.

reviews.author: Tim Brayton
reviews.text: An absurdly grounding, centering experience. Just the project itself had a rewarding, methodical sturdiness - not the film, but the project, the decision Takahata Isao made to create an almost three-hour-long study of the canals of Yanagawa that goes into exhaustive detail on seemingly every possible topic for discussion: their history, their design and function, their ecological impact, their human-ecological impact, how they got dirty and how they are kept clean, and, not by any means as an afterthought, how they are extraordinarily beautiful and tourist-friendly. Sidebars include musings on how water features are managed across Japan, and the relative pros and cons of modern versus ancient environmental technologies. It's just so gratifying to watch something that is so quietly…

Isao Takahata has always been invested in telling environmentalist tales and this is no different! The fun little animated segments were spare, but charming and funny considering Studio Ghibli’s animated heavy future.

reviews.author: kuboa
reviews.text: By the end of the first hour I was convinced I had learned all there was to learn about Yanagawa’s canals. I was so wrong. There were nearly two more hours to go, and I savored every minute. Besides the gorgeous slice-of-life river scenery and the adorable animated explainers of how, e.g., sluice gates operate, the heart of this documentary is the struggle to reclaim centuries-old canals from pollution and despicable state planning that would turn them into sewers and bury them in concrete. Like all Studio Ghibli works, The Story of Yanagawa’s Canals is romantically conservative, evincing a passionate belief in the preservation of local nature and cultural customs — intertwined, in Takahata’s view — that, with the right nudge, could become reactionary but never really does. Instead it’s truly, genuinely wholesome. I wish we could have gotten an entire series of documentaries just as long and cozy as this one.

reviews.author: carrieandtracy
reviews.text: What in the hell happened to Richard Rush? The Stunt Man is so sophisticated and funny, shot with such elan — it’s just freaking weird that the guy’s career very nearly stops, right there. All the performances have real depth. Mr. O’Toole is the obvious MVP, but Mr. Railsback and Ms. Hershey do their own heavy lifting. There is a scene, late in the film, between the two of them that would never make it on the screen today. Producers would think it’s too long, too late in the movie, “right when we should be ratcheting up,” and it would be drastically cut. But it’s actually a smart, well-written, beautifully performed (theatrical) scene that allows us greater investment in the characters before their lives are put in danger for the climax.

reviews.text: Hot on the heels of “The Brutalist,” Mona Fastvold and Brady Corbet have returned with another sweeping historical epic about a European iconoclast who comes to America in order to build a new kind of church. Even more excitingly, “The Testament of Ann Lee” — a speculative, feverish, and altogether rapturous biopic about the Mancunian preacher who founded the Shakers and believed herself to be the female incarnation of Christ on Earth — addresses the most glaring problem with last year’s story about the fictional architect László Tóth: It wasn’t a musical.

reviews.text: This is how you make a feel-good film. No cheaply manufactured emotions, just beautiful, humane observation of a growing relationship between two people on the run from the world outside. It loses its composition in the second half (mostly because of a bizarre shift in the story), but the humor and chemistry between Helena Bohnam Carter and Kenneth Branagh stay strong. Those two's chemistry seems to come just as effortlessly as breathing. So bad that Branagh came from magnificent Shakespeare adaptations and inspired films, and ended as a grotesque villain in "Tenet" and directs straight-to-DVD crap like "Artemis Foul". I keep my fingers crossed for his career to skyrocket again.

reviews.text: The Things You Kill is a brooding, elliptical study of grief, inheritance, and the cyclical nature of violence—familial and otherwise. Directed by Alireza Khatami, the film follows Ali (Ekin Koç), a literature professor whose quiet life in rural Turkey unravels after the suspicious death of his ailing mother. Grief quickly gives way to revelation as Ali begins to suspect his estranged, abusive father may have been behind it.The most interesting thematic here is the idea of transformation as a kind of self-erasure. In one of his lectures, Ali explains that the Arabic root of "translate"—rajama—can also mean "to kill." It's a potent metaphor for the film itself: to carry oneself across the abyss of trauma is to kill the…

This review is filled with spoilers, because there's no other way to explain the sheer brilliance on display here. So do turn back if you haven't seen it yet or continue forward knowing the risk.

reviews.author: claira curtis
reviews.text: The comparisons to Lynch aren’t off-base, but they do feel a bit lacking in defining what’s here. The frightening eeriness of how events escalate over the course of the film is very effective. The Things You Kill really sinks itself down into its most haunting, unnerving spaces, using these emotionally charged moments to needle into grief and duty and the weight of expectation. I ultimately felt personally removed from a lot of what’s here, but I never lost a sense of curiosity over where this was choosing to go within its narrative and larger thematic takeaways. Very possible there are degrees of depth here that I missed entirely. The final few minutes have an especially exciting way of leaving a chill down the spine that I appreciated. There’s a shot within the film that utilizes a mirror that had my jaw hanging open.

reviews.author: Sam Jalali
reviews.text: Alireza Khatami just knows his way to leaving a viewer completely dazed, but I think the brilliance of watching a film like this comes solely from how he’s able to hide a gut-wrenching social critique inside a surrealist puzzle. This isn't just the case for the film’s "twisty" narrative, but also in the way it feels like Lost Highway if it were directed by Abbas Kiarostami and a dreamlike, Lynchian haze that somehow feels grounded by a heavy, earthly reality.

reviews.author: Josh Lewis
reviews.text: I have a running theory that the truest, purest capital-C cinema is really just any movie that prominently features a train—both literally and symbolically. Anyway by that measure this is the best movie of all time. At one point two real trains crash into each other and it's not even the most impressive, large-scale destruction Franekenheimer shoots in this inky, perfectly-composed ode to the tangible mechanics of history (drawn in natural landscapes vs. steel, oil, soot, and steam) and the sweaty, bleeding men who operate them. Art is an expression of beauty, of life; a dream of a world beyond war, labor, machinery, untold misery, and death. Unfortunately, we're not there yet.

reviews.author: Nakul
reviews.text: John Frankenheimer's THE TRAIN is a goddamn masterpiece. A big scale yet taut & tight adrenaline-fueled action flick that leaves you at the edge of your seat until the very end. It's crazy how much of a spectacle and how much fun the film is, despite the grim premise. Also the movie feels very modern, especially with its characterizations of the protagonist and antagonist. Frankenheimer used real locations, no models, big explosions, and real crashes. They actually blew up a train depot to shoot that one scene. Burt Lancaster does crazy dangerous stunts, he actually injured his leg sliding down a ladder, the limp he has towards the end of the film is real. I can’t wait to watch this again.

reviews.author: comrade_yui
reviews.text: frankenheimer's style is heavy and loud, but easy to appreciate -- the luxuriant deep focus recreation of WW2 french/german trainyards gives the train a half-prestigious feel, one step in jean-pierre melville territory, another step near the dadcore canon. the astonishing use of real locomotives and all the associated engineering thereof goes a long way towards cementing this as a vulgar classic -- there's no better practical effect than watching actual trains getting smashed into each other and blown the hell up (we used to build things in -- sorry, destroy things, in other countries). there's barely any musical score to this film, which is why i think chris mcquarrie enjoys it so much -- no artificial catharsis, no audience hand-holding,…

reviews.text: The Truffle Hunters has a great subject—aging Italian foragers and their dogs, carrying on the storied tradition of searching forests for the rare fungi—but its true strength is in its compositions. Directors Michael Dweck and Gregory Kershaw, who also handle the cinematography, frame and light these men as if they were sitting for Rembrandt or Vermeer. And so two friends share hunting memories while sitting in a dank cellar, a shaft of light illuminating their reverie. Another subject sits at a table of towering tomatoes, his head peering just above the pile in a comical still life. reviews.author: Enfant du Siècle
reviews.text: An intimate drama about the life and tribulations of three sisters who attend a café in Hanoi. This is a very natural and sensory work in which Tran Anh Hung, with a subtle and delicate eye, takes us to the warm Vietnamese summer and make us feel the crystalline rain, and perceive the flavours and scents of his land. The stories he tells, about the everyday life of a family, their longings and concerns, are of great simplicity, like life itself that flows slowly. Through this vivid mosaic, the director reflects on marriage, family and relationships, but above all on happiness, and portrays Vietnamese society and the role of women in it. The Vertical Ray of the Sun is a quiet film about the little moments that shape life and create harmony within it.

reviews.author: Pretentious Film Critic
reviews.text: A dream where plot dissolves, and emotion becomes weather: how affection ripens into routine, how desire quiets into companionship, how closeness can turn into distance without anyone "doing" anything. The film watches three women move through partnership like through shifting light, and slowly suggests that the deepest intimacy isn’t always between man and woman. Pregnancy, dancing, and small confessions of intimacy culminate in bitter revelations about forging connection while drifting to the edges, present but not fully reachable, like figures behind a curtain. The film lets rooms speak. Afternoon sun becomes private narration, a lush language that says what the characters refuse to name. Love doesn’t arrive as a declaration here. It returns as a pattern of separation, convergence, and recognition.

reviews.author: Filipe Furtado
reviews.text: Backstage drama about an up-and-coming rock band with the expected amount of romantic, drug-related, and internal strife troubles. Cannon produced this, one of the multiple youth-oriented movies on this vein they put out that never got the attention some of their action stuff did. It is fairly corny, but makes the good decision to keep the scales low, and the songs are believable as the work of people with enough talent to get noticed. Clancy Brown is enjoyable, as he always is, but most of the characters aren’t very distinct, and the lead is a bore. Writer/director JS Cardone usually does thrillers, and he struggles a little at the more grounded moments, but this is warm and pleasant, if very inessential.

reviews.author: Rafael "Mister Movie" Jovine
reviews.text: This is one of those tragic tales I've heard before but never knew the full facts of; it's the kind of story that does more than just crush your heart; it also makes you question humanity, or at least, certain groups. Beyond the premise, you have an excellent lead performance from Danielle Deadwyler, who manages in many ways to elevate the film by conveying the few moments of happiness despite the great emotional hit, both personal and maternal, that she endured, making one believe her every tear and pain.

reviews.author: nick
reviews.text: Devastating and necessary, Till is a dazzling celebration of a legendary black woman who turned her bone-crushing trauma into a never-ending drive to battle racism. Danielle Deadwyler is such a force of nature playing the titular character in this heartbreaking story that's equal parts historical and personal. In a scenario where histrionics is mostly excused, Deadwyler has offered her own version of a quite restrained yet sympathetic Mamie Till. Director Chinonye Chukwu was equally efficient with her efforts to rid of the genre tropes, via a dynamic camera work and style.

reviews.text: Till doesn't contain many moments of spectacular or innovative filmmaking but Chinonye Chukwu is smart enough to give her superb cast the room to play out events with emotional honesty and sensitivity. Danielle Deadwyler gives a flawless performance as Mamie Till-Mobley, her face wearing the pain that should never have been endured, as well boundless strength and courage. Though the film sometimes feels too similar to other biographical dramas, both aesthetically and structurally, it's hard not to be invested in this competently told fight for justice.

reviews.author: Filipe Furtado
reviews.text: 21st century cinema's big bang. An act of renewal obsessed with what one can makes of the past and future legacies. Tsui's seems decided to rethink a lot of the local cinema's tradition from the past two decades (there's many nods to New Wave classics starting with Tsui's own Dangerous Encounters First Kind, to WKW films and John Woo's bullet ballet). The over-the-top action (and the back half is one major set piece after another) keeps finding new spins on old scenarios, some of the most creative and large action scenes around. The editing is some of Tsui's most intense and unusual. I wish Wu Bai was a bit more animated performer, but I love how his character seems able to do anything. Artifice rules everything to the point I'm never sure if the Brazilian bad guys speaking Spanish was intentional or a goof. So wild, a baby chord getting cut with teeth isn't even among the more memorable parts.

reviews.author: reibureibu
reviews.text: Videogames of the aughts as reflected in cinema of the aughts, its inspiration and precursor embracing such newfound vulgarity. The emergence of three-dimensional games brought with it an exploration of what could be done in such spatial terms, the Z-axis taking the X- and Y- and creating immersive-if-simple architectural spaces for us to explore. Super Mario 64 was momentous for doing exactly this and nothing more, yet this feat alone completely changed the medium.

reviews.author: reibureibu
reviews.text: Where normally Hark opts for a complete stylistic density and maximalism what becomes especially notable here is in how he strips away sound in some of the most action-packed moments both visually and kinetically. Initially it is odd to witness a scene of two men in a struggle for death as they wield a gun and sledgehammer and even potted plant against each other and all one can hear is the sound of their pitter-patter of dress shoes on linoleum flooring, and breaths. The little intimates heard in quietude, jarring here in juxtaposing violence. But rather than being drowned out by incidental noise this instead pulls us in closer to these characters' experience, adrenaline stripping out all else but the barest we need to survive: the echoes of their feet, the swinging of their fists, the click of their gun, and the beating of your heart.

reviews.text: Tomahawk isn't a particularly good western, but it is a notable one for its unfailingly sympathetic portrait of the Sioux people, and the violence that results from their mistreatment by both the American government and white settlers. The villain of the piece is an unrepentant killer of Indigenous people who joined the American military purely to have an excuse to do so, while all of those with any degree of intelligence understand that, when the Sioux become violent, it is because they, themselves, have been victims of violence.

Sherman's film has some fine performances, not just from Heflin, but Yvonne De Carlo, Alex Nicol, and a small cameo from Rock Hudson too.

reviews.text: Al inicio de Tomahawk, Sherman filma a un sioux tocando un tambor desde lo alto de una roca. Entonces la cámara empieza a describir un movimiento panorámico desde esa roca hasta la llanura (donde hay sioux y soldados americanos) atravesando el cielo nublado. En el cine de Sherman, las nubes parecen un lugar sagrado, lleno de belleza y que el director filma de forma devota. Después, Sherman muestra en panorámicas y en maravillosos travellings a las tropas, tanto sioux como yankees allí reunidas. Durante la firma del tratado de Fort Laramie, por la que los Estados Unidos limitaron aún más el territorio Sioux. Y Sherman, con su mirada ambiciosa, sus movimientos gigantescos, parece decirnos que la historia de un país…

reviews.text: Jim Bridger, the famous trapper and scout, mediates a meeting between the Sioux and the US Cavalry over the plan to build a road through Indian territory so that whites can get to gold deposits in Montana. It's set up to put your focus on the string of broken treaties and genocide carried out by racist elements. The themes couldn't be more controversial and Tomahawk doesn't dodge them while also introducing Yvonne De Carlo as a traveling performer who falls for Bridger played by Van Heflin but is sought after by the despicable Lieutenant Rob Dancy played by Alex Nicol. However Bridger's wife is a Cheyenne woman played by Susan Cabot. It sounds superfluous to the issues but actually integrates…

reviews.author: Filipe Furtado
reviews.text: Somber liberal western. Some (offscreen) white men want profit, some (onscreen) white men just plain hate and scout Van Heflin is left trying to mediate inevitable conflict giving peaceful advice for weak uninterested authorities for whom bloody conflict is just business as usual. Strong balanced script, wonderful cinematography and some good action. Director George Sherman natural instincts are for action more than discourse, but he has a strong feeling for the genre darker instincts. Tomahawk next to last scene is one of the most unpleasant action scenes on American movies, a long protacted massacre.

In a way, that's not all negative, because the toned down experience fit the mood of the characters involved.

reviews.author: Doug Dibbern
reviews.text: This is one of those liberal post-war Westerns that tries to take a balanced approach to the Indian wars of the American West. In this case, the script goes out of its way to be historically accurate, following events along the Bozeman Trail from 1866-1868, covering the Sand Creek Massacre, the Fetterman Fight, and the eventual abandonment of Fort Kearney due to the war wisdom of Red Cloud, one of the leaders of the Oglala Sioux. The protagonist is, of course, a white man, one of those in-between figures, Van Heflin as Jim Bridger, a mountain man whose Indian wife was killed by lawless, marauding whites, the type of guy who earnestly espouses great admiration for the Sioux people. The…

reviews.author: Evelyn Rose
reviews.text: "The white man's promises are written in water." A Universal-International western in Technicolor, directed by George Sherman with a sure eye for landscape and vivid colour. Van Heflin stars as a simmering kettle of cavalry-hating anti-racism, with support from Yvonne De Carlo, Jack Oakie, John War Eagle, Rock Hudson, and Susan Cabot. The film's most interesting feature, though, is its script by Silvia Richards and Maurice Geraghty. Among the earliest '50s westerns to reflect critically on American settler colonialism, I was expecting a message far less clear-cut than this. But the script doesn't mince words: the American cavalry tried to steal Lakota land, by legal subterfuge and military siege tactics, out of racialized contempt and greed for gold, and the…

reviews.author: Joseph Grimault
reviews.text: Five years before The Searchers came out, George Sherman's Tomahawk already offered a critical viewpoint on the processes and machinations of violence and racism used by the US to steal (and the film makes it very clear) the land of the Natives. This film however, is also the other side of the coin of John Ford's masterpiece: contrary to Ethan Edwards (John Wayne), Jim Bridger (Van Heflin) is seldomly seen using or firing a gun, let alone violence, the only two times we do see him, is in self-defense against a Native and with wrath against a white man; while Ethan Edwards is driven by hate towards the native people, Jim Bridger looks tearfully to the waves of Natives perishing…

reviews.text: An overall mild and uninspiring neo-noir B-film of the early 90s, reveling in its own cheap perfume, skanky hoes, and scummy dudes. For what it’s worth, I really quite like James Belushi as an actor, and here, he’s more than solid. What derides the film from success is its shoddy story and quite lackluster supporting cast—particularly that of Lorraine Bracco—who I was jazzed about seeing in a pre-Sopranos role. I even suspected she would fit the role of the femme fatale like a glove, which in actuality, could not have been farther from the truth. If you’re looking for a filthy, lived-in thriller with bursts of saxxy sax man blowing his heart out than you may find some minor entertainment here. Instead, you're stuck with the 2007 version of each. Tsui Hark was deep in one of his creative doldrums, and doesn't emerge until his first Detective Dee and his decisive turn toward mainland blockbusters. Ringo Lam had quit directing, having gotten tired of it and wanting to spend time with his family. This was the only movie he did between 2003 and 2015 and his heart still wasn't with it. Which leaves Johnnie To as the only one at the top…

reviews.text: Tsui Hark, Ringo Lam, and Johnnie To play a dizzying, breakneck game of exquisite corpse, Tsui launching the film’s hardluck trio into a hunt for buried treasure, Lam deciding where to take it next (nowhere good), and To taking the baton to wrap it all up. A messy, freewheeling modern fable about the futility of all things (at least concerning get-rich-quick schemes). “I’d rather take the money today! What if tomorrow I’m dead?” After the first two-thirds’ chaotic urban breakdown, To sends the sprawling cast of characters to a roadside diner in the countryside for a kind of collective moral reckoning; a gorgeously serene nocturnal ballet of gunplay and double-crosses, allegiances lost and gained with one swift glance. “When you…

reviews.author: Nick Newman
reviews.text: Surprised this has such a low rep — three of Hong Kong's biggest (best? in at least two-ish cases I don't know) doing a round-robin crime picture plotted to a perfect pitch of coherent sloppiness. Each section makes any excuse to keep the three lowlife idiots in the same frame. Lots of vital info revealed in wordless shots. Morality and honor and lack thereof, heroic bloodshed, cowardly bumbling — maybe doesn't take any of its concepts to a sublime point but all the while does just about everything you want from this kind of film.

reviews.author: Sean
reviews.text: In serious contention for the worst film concept in history. Taking three directors and forcing them to construct a single narrative without any communication past vague broad strokes of the plot and just seeing what happens??? Are you out of yer fahkin mind??? Anyways though this somehow manages to work because all the directors are great and it's really cool to see how obvious whose segment is whose(To and Tsui from my experience with their work, and Lam by process of elimination). To's segment is obviously my favorite(jeez is it noticeable how far ahead he is in terms of compositions/framing/lighting/blocking), but Tsui's is fun too. I didn’t enjoy Lam's, but it was aight all things considered. Didn’t get too much out of this as a whole because, frankly, it's a fuckin trainwreck, but these guys are way too good at what they do for me not to get a kick out of it. Fun stuff! Incoherent, sure, but fun nonetheless.

reviews.author: Matt Singer
reviews.text: Not an especially comprehensive biopic, and not really an exciting business story either. (I knew nothing about Preston Tucker, and I basically knew how the film would end before I watched a single frame.) Tucker: The Man and His Dream pretty much only works as allegory; as Francis Ford Coppola, the iconoclast who dreamed of making things his way outside the established system, telling his own story through Preston Tucker, who suffered much the same fate as Coppola in the world of automobiles. But it’s a damn good allegory. And it’s amazing how much sadder Tucker is simply because Tucker (at least as played by Jeff Bridges) was such a happy person.

reviews.author: Brian Formo
reviews.text: Tucker: The Man and His Dream is a loving ode to the American build-it mentality that created immense prosperity post-WWII, but also created a wall to not let new competition enter the fold once prosperity had been consolidated to “enough companies.” Tucker (Jeff Bridges) designed cars that should have been allowed to compete with the Big Three (Ford, General Motors, and Chrysler) but their bigness gave way to big corporate protections within the very halls of government. Think of the last two big bailouts this century and how many potential Tuckers and their dreams have gone unrealized because the U.S. government favors the establishment. Too Big to Fail first set its teeth in America post-FDR.

reviews.text: According to IMDb trivia this movie “Was made as a benefit movie with the proceeds going to the Hong Kong Directors Guild.” Interesting and it somewhat explains the uneven end product. Twin Dragons was directed by both Tsui Hark and Ringo Lam. The film feels a bit different than the typical Jackie Chan movie of the time. More gun violence and Jackie even gets laid in this one. The action especially in the finale is pretty good and the comedy funny enough to mildly entertain. I would not call this a great movie and it is far from Jackie’s best but definitely watchable and entertaining enough at least for fans of the star. What is also fun is to watch out for the many cameos by other stars and director. Not a must-watch but the new Blu-ray Edition from 88 Films is pretty great and worth getting it you are a fan of the movie or Jackie.

reviews.author: More_Badass
reviews.text: You see that title and poster, and think “identical twin antics, got it”. But that doesn’t prepare you for the 100%-Ringo Lam-certified hospital chaos, or how a wild speedboat chase ends with Looney Tunes physics, or that a hefty amount of comedy isn’t just from mistaken identity mishaps but also psychic connection slapstick. Twin Dragons gets a lot of humorous situational mileage out of its contrasting Jackie Chans, and the action - when it happens - is never less than entertaining. Neither full Hark wacky nor full Lam intense, but just enough silliness, destruction, and vintage Chan to be inventive and impressive. The dockyard/car factory finale is a top-notch capper for this action-comedy

reviews.author: Darren Carver-Balsiger
reviews.text: History is the most important cornerstone of society. Not a single moment of our choices, our culture, our entire lives isn't determined by what came before. Anyone ignorant of history is ignorant of far greater things. There is not a single cultural work - a film, a song, a painting - that cannot be examined historically. They can all be examined by what cultural and social history proceeded them, and also by how history has subsequently judged them. Most films pretend to ignore history, but even the shallowest of them - superhero movies, horror b-movies, style-over-substance arthouse pictures - are indicative of the culture around them. To judge films in a vacuum is to ignore their most meaningful purpose: the…

reviews.text: One question dogged United 93 when it came out that led to a number of critics underrating it initially. No one could deny the intense, visceral power of Paul Greengrass's film, the queasy realism and punch-to-the-gut human drama of it, but considering the fact that the movie tends to leave one feeling gutted, drained and wrung out like a soggy gym sock, the question that wasn't immediately answered was: WHY? Yes, the film is a documentary-style recreation of what is believed to have happened on United Flight 93 on September 11th, but really, what's the point of making a movie like that? reviews.author: Tim Fehrenbach
reviews.text: “you never can trust nobody no more.”Released in 1954, Robert Aldrich’s Vera Cruz was a new kind of western – not a mythic saga about cowboys and righteous codes, but a sharp, cynical pivot away from the genre’s classical morality, exposing the corruption at the heart of the traditional western. After seeing Aldrich’s genre-bending Kiss Me Deadly, one of my favorites, I was already primed for subversive grittiness – and yes, Vera Cruz delivers. It’s startlingly modern for its time: a story of fractured characters driven by greed and shifting allegiances, set against a backdrop of eroding social order.

reviews.author: comrade_yui
reviews.text: perfect, perfect, absolutely perfect, has the dignity and craft of a classic western with the rugged anarchism of a revisionist western, the best of both worlds, with loads of character actors and future stars in the cast: jack elam, charles bronson, ernest borgnine, henry brandon, cesar romero, i mean come on, if you're a fan of these films this is a no-brainer masterpiece just from reading those names alone. the pacing is air-tight, it's packed with gunfights and action, excellent tough-guy dialogue, political commentary, complex characters and relationships; vera cruz is a stunner, an essential text in the history of its genre. cannot recommend it enough!

reviews.author: Peter Labuza
reviews.text: Was worried at first that Lancaster was going to out act Gary Cooper, whose working in High Noon territory despite the film being quite the opposite, but soon levels into a fascinating duo. Could make a great double feature with Duck, You Sucker!, as both are films about people exploiting the Mexican revolution for their own gain. Film is filled with utter delights, especially as the gang infiltrates what's essentially the set of a Visconti movie and acts like a gang of slobs. Double and triple crosses abound in what could essentially be a film noir (Cooper is a veteran of the war), with banter up there with the stuff in Double Indemnity. Falters near the finish mark, as Aldrich gets a soft heart for a good cause, but the fact that Lancaster can't help but smile throughout the movie, even in his final moment, makes this essential viewing, especially for die-hards fans of the actor.
