reviews.author: Colin the dude
reviews.text: Often cited as one of the premiere precursors to the Spaghetti Western and the movement toward gritty, ruthless Westerns that would define the genre henceforth, it is clear that Vera Cruz helped initiate the blurring of lines between good and evil in Western protagonists. Even sweeter, it is a perfect crossbreeding of the traditional hero and the antihero, portrayed by Gary Cooper and Burt Lancaster, respectively. You could call it a passing of the torch for the new breed of hero to come. It is also a fast-paced, fast-cutting film, helping to mold the new action standard of quick cutting to accentuate the chaos of violence. Shooting entirely on location in the Mexican wasteland benefits the film tenfold in establishing…

reviews.author: HKFanatic
reviews.text: "Vera Cruz" is a tight, 90-minute Western full of character, intrigue, and action. By flirting with nihilism, Robert Aldrich's film points the way towards the spaghetti Westerns to come, with Burt Lancaster as a proto-Man in Black. But, shot on location in Mexico, what "Vera Cruz" might have going for it most is an authentic milieu: following lethal men for whom the Civil War meant little more than a reversal of fortune, hardened men of arms who now find themselves alone in a foreign land, taking part in another people's war, not out of a sense of duty or honor but for cold hard coin.

reviews.author: Gregor Kreyca
reviews.text: Vera Cruz is a good but not great Western in my opinion. It’s short, mostly entertaining and has some impressive action set-pieces. The cast is good but while I love Cooper and Lancaster individually, I don’t think they make for a very compelling screen pairing. There are quite a few familiar faces in the supporting cast but due to the short runtime they don’t really get much room to shine. It’s really not a bad film and certainly worth a watch for Western fans but I would not call it a career highlight of anyone involved.

reviews.text: To me a really great example of originality and provocation meaning very little if a film doesn’t deliver on its presented ideas, it’s more interesting in structure than content but even the shifting POV doesn’t amount to much. There’s a stretch in the middle (the best part imo) between a disgruntled cop and a young troublemaker where Cregger seems to be introducing elements of coincidence, human fallibility, and even how our institutions can fail to protect our kids, but otherwise the whole Magnolia thing is mostly a gimmick to control when information is revealed. There are so many intriguing dynamics in this town that are ultimately dead-ended in service of a ~crazy~ third act that people will hoot and holler about, but despite more sophisticated filmmaking after Barbarian this feels even more fractured in its ambitions. Many more thoughts… didn’t hate it but didn’t get much out of it either.

reviews.author: Filipe Furtado
reviews.text: Classic Hong scenario: you meet your girlfriend's family, things seem to go relatively well, then you sit at the table, start to drink, and embarrassment ensues. Of course, things haven't gone that well; the casualness of the filmmaking and the light comic tone play against an inherent violent tension that is generational and class-oriented. After the relatively elaborate By the Stream, this is Hong back into his more offhand late mode, and the writing is among his most straightforward. It does arrive at a powerful place; most late Hong are about reaching those moments of departure. The big table scene is wonderful, and the main character is among his more intriguing figures in his mix of silliness and feeling.

The beauty of nature evoking the nature of beauty. Or is it the other way around?

reviews.text: I've seen a lot of college-frat-beach-sex-nerd-whatever comedies from the 80's and it's not that often that you find one that's professionally made as well as being fun as hell. Even the music is good in this, damn good, where most similar films tend to either make me want to tear my ears off or laugh uncontrollably. Also, fucking Francine from American Dad is one of the ladies here. Huzzahwuuuhhh? Most remarkable is that the four main characters all feel like developed characters. They have personalities and have different goals and wants in life, yet they all feel like they would be best friends in real life. That's the ticket to the movie being as endearing as it is. The film is a nice example of how no matter what genre it may be, there will always be examples of how to do said genre right.

We focus on a big secluded house in the country, inhabited by a mature lesbian and her photographer "nephew". After being spurned by her last lover, auntie invites over a new girl for fun and games. The film has a dual narrative - one focusing on the deviant pair seducing the young model, and the other following a lacklustre investigation into the whereabouts of the previous house guest. It works really well. The three central characters are well defined and the interplay between them is great and culminates in a couple of surprisingly sexy scenes.…

reviews.text: Sara (Pia Andersson) and her nephew Theo (Karl Lanchbury) are both photographers living in the country. They invite a young woman called Tulia (Vivien Neves) to stay with them for the weekend. The aim is to have her pose for photographs for Theo...and for sexy time. Oh not just between Theo and Tulia, Sara is disturbingly in the mix too. This is definitely more on the erotic side rather then horror or even thriller. It's hard to take seriously given that Theo looks a lot like MadTV's Stuart, well that and the copious amounts of nudity. Although it isn't very long, it's not very well paced at all so it's a bit of a slog unfortunately. It's an unusual exploitation film, I'll give it that but as far as José Ramón Larraz films go, I thought Symptoms was so much better. If we are talking about movies with water related devices in the title, The Swimming Pool was much better.

reviews.text: The Lucky Stars were a supergroup of popular Hong Kong comic actors led by Sammo Hung. Their first three movies also featured Jackie Chan in a supporting role, and were sold around the world on his presence. For Chan scholars, this one is most notable for a scene where he rollerskates under a moving truck. The action is incredible when it comes, although this is not just an action movie. When I was a teen, I used to find these movies exasperating for their heavy reliance on goofy comedy. Now I'm older and wiser and can appreciate a scene where Richard Ng thinks he's turned himself invisible and so walks around a busy house nude.

reviews.text: "Winter Days" (冬の日, Fuyu no Hi) has got to be one of the best animated anthologies of all time. It is a perfect marriage of form and intention.

Can't imagine myself rewatching this as a whole but would rather pick out individual segments, like the one from Yuri Norstein.

reviews.author: soulmass218
reviews.text: Recently finished a rewatch of this TV series after around two decades since originally seeing it. While the world and character design by CLAMP are a treat for the eyes as always, harkening back to that wonderful 90s anime aesthetic (even though this aired in 2001), I can't help but dock points for significant padding in the actual storytelling. Yoshiaki Kawajiri is a legendary director, but you can tell he was working with too little material to spread across 24 episodes here. reviews.author: Zak Shannon
reviews.text: X is an action-packed dark fantasy epic that does a fairly impressive job of translating Clamp’s original manga series to the small screen. Yoshiaki Kawajiri’s first and only foray into directing TV anime is a pretty solid debut. Naoki Satō‘s score is powerful and bombastic with many unforgettable tracks, but they are often overused and can feel out of place during certain scenes. ‘X’ has a large roster of characters that are surprisingly well-rounded and each are given a decent amount of screen time. The final stretch of episodes do feel like they’re rushing pieces off the board in time for the series’ conclusion, but despite that hiccup, Yoshiaki Kawajiri’s ‘X’ is a satisfying enough adaptation.

reviews.author: Filipe Furtado
reviews.text: Much like Peking Opera Blues nearly three decades earlier this is blockbuster as a matter of politics. Freedom of movement, color and imagination just adds to film’s overall trust. This is even better on the big screen and Tsui remain a master of moving between registers: detective story, fantasy, period chamber politics, action and low brow satirical comedy, everything is game and possible. The big final set piece is one of the best sustained action scenes of the last few years. Late Tsui might be uneven but when he is on, like in the Dee films nobody makes popular filmmaking with such scope under and subversive edge.

reviews.author: Sean Gilman
reviews.text: The anarchist prankster Tsui Hark who burst onto the Hong Kong scene over 30 years ago with Dangerous Encounters - First Kind and We're Going to Eat You still lurks underneath layers of glossy CGI as the eponymous detective, in order to counter-act their poisoned tea, orders all 1200 members of the Tang Dynasty Imperial household to drink bowls of eunuch urine.

reviews.author: Shea
reviews.text: Absolutely love the integration of CGI and real sets here - it's not exactly seamless, but it's gorgeous! The action is as thrillingly imaginative as any I've seen, utilising everything from random bits of furniture and attacking insects to green screen and triple exposure effects. A few moments that really made my jaw drop! Though this isn't particularly humourous (apart from one epic extended gag) there's a buoyant sense of adventure that compliments the tragic romance and political intrigue, and as cartoonish as it can get, it's pretty beautifully balanced. The more stuff like this we get in the West, the better.

Tsui Hark trades a coherent narrative with wire work to feast your eyes upon but hanging by said wire is the root of Zu: Warriors from the Magic Mountain, a basic tale of good vs. evil, rivals against two armies, humans ruining the earth and a strong-willed Yuen Biao, who finds himself in the confines of a supernatural playground; fighting off ghost demons with glowing blue eyes,…

reviews.author: comrade_yui
reviews.text: 110% dynamite wuxia anarchy. tsui hark operates on a completely different level than most filmmakers, it's hard to even describe what he exactly does outside of just having a far-reaching mastery of how things should be framed, moved, edited, paced, whatever, he's got it handled and more than deserves a comparison to spielberg for these formal chops. he takes a well-worn genre known for its palatial intrigue & opera-based choreography and adds about ten tons of flying swords, explosions and laser beams into the mix, he makes a 95 minute film feel like it contains 4 hours worth of epic storytelling, he upends any sense of filmic decorum and instead gives us this eye-popping extravaganza that doesn't fail to entertain for even a second. very few movies can even muster the bravery to try what this does, much less succeed in matching its sheer audaciousness.
